stories.body:
John Aloisi’s side need a point on the final day to seal their maiden title – but their form has dropped off a cliff

W ith four games of the Chinese Super League to go, Chengdu Rongcheng needed just a point to clinch their first title. With one game to go, they still need a point. What was a formality has become a formidable task. The biggest bottle job in Asian football history is very much on and it would be as popular as it would be dramatic.

The coach of the Sichuan club, the former Portsmouth and Coventry striker John Aloisi, has seen a 12-point lead over Dalian Yingbo cut to just three before Sunday’s showdowns. Whatever happens, this is a positive and thrilling end to a season that started negatively – literally – with nine of the 16 top-tier clubs kicking off on minus points. They had been punished as part of a “special campaign to crack down on match-fixing, gambling and corruption in the football industry”, said a joint statement from the Chinese Football Association, the Ministry of Public Security and the General Administration of Sport at the time.

Chengdu were one of the seven to start on zero, above the defending champions, Shanghai Port, who lost five points and the runners-up, Shanghai Shenhua, who were hit with 10. It robbed the usual favourites of energy and it was all a bit surreal.

It almost felt over as soon as it started with Chengdu opening up a big lead, dropping just two points from the first 12 games while the usual powers struggled to get going.

Chengdu is a major city more known for its fiery Sichuan cuisine, genteel temples and cute pandas than football, despite English attempts to change that. In 2006, Sheffield United bought a local club but the Chengdu Blades were eventually dissolved in 2015. Four years later, City Football Group bought a stake in Sichuan Jiuniu but then moved the club to the southern city of Shenzhen in 2024.

Chengdu Rongcheng were formed in 2018, coming up through the divisions to finally, this season, be within touching distance of the championship. But just two wins from the last 13 and three straight defeats mean the leaders are not limping to the line but have collapsed right next to it.

It should have been over weeks ago. On 10 October, more than 40,000 fans were ready to celebrate the title but an added-time goal from Alberto Quiles gave Tianjin Jinmen Tiger a 1-0 win and postponed the celebrations. Next up was a trip to Shanghai Port but that ended in a 3-0 defeat. The penultimate game of the season came against challengers Dalian Yingbo, when again, just avoiding defeat was needed. It was another painful experience as they lost 1-0 after missing a first-half penalty and having a 90th-minute equaliser ruled out by the video assistant referee.

Chengdu have not scored in almost seven hours of football while Dalian are the form team with four consecutive wins. If they win a fifth against Tianjin then Chengdu need a point at fourth-placed Shandong Taishan as the league is decided by head-to-head results before goal difference. Not many think they will. Even fewer hope so. Dalian and the 60,000 fans that attend home games are the people’s choice. Chengdu are not popular because their fans have developed a poor reputation. Last November, the club was fined about $70,000 (£52,200) after some home supporters racially abused Henan FC’s Ghanaian striker Frank Acheampong, just weeks after a punishment of $3,000 after travelling supporters at a Champions League game in South Korea threw bottles at the Ulsan HD players.

Whatever happens it is an unexpected and dramatic ending to a season that started in shock and the usual negative international headlines that surround Chinese football. The grandstand finish is welcome and average attendances have risen. They are set to finish at about 30,000, a considerable jump from last season’s 25,755 and, by some distance, the best in Asia. Regional leagues have been enjoying some popularity too, showing that there is genuine love for the game in the country; a passion that grows better when it is organic from the bottom rather than organised from the top.

after newsletter promotion

The national side is still a problem, though, and even for a fanbase well accustomed to disappointment the recent 5-0 defeat to Palestine at home, the fourth-biggest loss in history, was tough to take. As one journalist said, being thrashed by Brazil, Japan and Wales is one thing, but Palestine was another. There were some mitigating circumstances in that a number of national team players were at the Asian Games, where China actually performed well, losing narrowly to old nemesis South Korea in the bronze final.

There are signs that the gap behind Korea is not as wide as it used to be. China reached the final of the under-17 and under-23 Asian championships this year before losing both against Japan. Compared with the rest of Asia’s best, young Chinese players are closing the gap at a technical and tactical level. Exporting more players to Europe is necessary to play at a higher level and if that happens, that senior national shirt may feel a little lighter.

Failure can, however, be hard to shake off as Chengdu Rongcheng may well find out if they mess this up.

stories.title: California fights "preposterous" Trump admin demand to scrap state broadband laws
stories.summary: State tries to obtain broadband funds despite rejecting Trump admin condition.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
State tries to obtain broadband funds despite rejecting Trump admin condition.

California is accepting $1.42 billion in broadband grant funding from the Trump administration, but the state is not accepting the Trump administration’s demand that it stop enforcing a net neutrality law and other telecom regulations.

California’s stand against the Trump administration could result in multiple legal battles involving the state, federal government, and Internet providers seeking government funds. Although California told the federal government it would accept the money, it is reserving the right to challenge the condition imposed by the US. The state could delay or cancel plans to distribute broadband grants depending on how the process unfolds.

The National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) decided last year that states must agree not to enforce any rate regulation or net neutrality rule on ISPs that receive money from the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program. California had to decide whether to accept its share of the fund despite that restriction. California is slated to spend $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations, and may ultimately receive up to $1.86 billion from BEAD for a mix of deployment and non-deployment projects.

State officials argue that California should be able to obtain the money and keep enforcing its laws because the Trump administration’s demand would violate the state’s constitutional rights. The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) made its view clear in a carefully worded letter yesterday to Assistant Secretary of Commerce and NTIA Administrator Arielle Roth.

“The CPUC cannot be bound by any terms or conditions that are unconstitutional or not authorized by law and it expressly does not waive or concede any arguments or challenges concerning the legality, interpretation, or applicability of any term or condition,” CPUC President John Reynolds told Roth.

Reynolds’ letter also said the CPUC cannot prevent other California agencies from enforcing state laws, suggesting that the attorney general would maintain the right to punish misbehaving Internet providers.

California fighting “preposterous demand”

Reynolds’ letter acknowledged that the NTIA may not agree with the CPUC’s stance and said the state thus will not distribute any funding to ISPs until after the state and federal agency sort out any differences. If the NTIA refuses to change its position, California could sue the Trump administration on the grounds that the condition is unconstitutional.

The NTIA does not appear likely to bend. “As noted in the Department’s response to CPUC, the terms and conditions of the award constitute the entire agreement between NTIA and CPUC. No part of the letter outlining CPUC’s concerns is incorporated into or made part of the award,” an NTIA spokesperson told Ars today.

Consumer advocacy group Public Knowledge supported CPUC’s position . The Trump administration’s demand to preempt state laws is “brazen and meritless,” the group said.

“This administration’s preposterous demand that industry be given a blanket waiver from affordability requirements, net neutrality and privacy protections, and any other commitments to connect and serve Americans has no basis in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA), which established BEAD. And, as the commission points out, the NTIA has no authority to alter California state law or require California agencies to not enforce the law,” said Raza Panjwani, senior policy counsel at Public Knowledge.

The CPUC voted to ratify the funding plan in September. But Reynolds said in yesterday’s letter to the Trump administration that his agency’s acceptance of the funds is “based on the CPUC’s best understanding of the effect of Section 50” of the BEAD terms and conditions . Section 50 of the BEAD rules says each state:

shall commit that it will not enforce any law, regulation, order, contracting requirement, or other enforceable obligation that directly or indirectly regulates the rates, terms, and conditions of broadband Internet service… or imposes net neutrality rules, open access, or other utility-style rules on broadband Internet service, against a Subgrantee or its affiliates anywhere it provides service within the State (i.e., both BEAD and non-BEAD locations), while that Subgrantee has any subgrant that is still within its period of performance, extended period of performance, or federal interest period.

The BEAD rules specify that a net neutrality rule is one prohibiting ISPs from “blocking content, throttling speeds, imposing data caps, or engaging in paid prioritization.” ISPs obtaining BEAD funding could be exempt from such laws for up to 14 years.

California calls US rule “vague and ambiguous”

Reynolds’ letter said the NTIA-imposed condition is “vague and ambiguous as to its scope and its relationship to Section 47 U.S.C. § 1702(g)(2)(A)(i) of the BEAD statute,” the US law that created the BEAD program. He wrote:

The CPUC does not interpret Section 50 to require the CPUC to waive, release, or otherwise forfeit any rights, claims, arguments, or defenses concerning potential implications of Section 50 that may violate applicable laws. Further, the CPUC’s acceptance of funds under this award should not be understood as agreement either to refrain from compliance with mandatory legal duties or obligations, or to constrain other State of California entities in the exercise of their authorities to enforce state law, which is outside the scope of the CPUC’s authority. Moreover, California’s net neutrality law expressly provides that “any waiver of the provisions of this title is contrary to public policy and shall be unenforceable and void.” Likewise, many of the CPUC’s own programs that touch on broadband Internet access service are mandated by the California Public Utilities Code, and are neither discretionary nor waivable.

The NTIA today updated its BEAD progress dashboard to reflect that California has signed its final agreement with the federal agency. California was the last state or territory to turn in its final agreement.

“All 56 states and territories have signed and returned their award agreement, finalizing the process,” the NTIA’s updated dashboard page said.

ISPs could insist state laws are invalid

California could face legal problems if and when it distributes the money, which is to be given to Internet service providers in exchange for deploying broadband in unserved and underserved areas. ISPs could insist that they don’t have to follow state law and sue California, or simply decide to violate consumer protection laws and defend against any lawsuits the state attorney general might file against them.

Reynolds apparently hopes to avoid that outcome by holding discussions with the NTIA to resolve any disagreement over the enforceability of California state law.

“To the extent that NTIA and the CPUC disagree about the CPUC’s obligations under Section 50 and other terms and conditions, the CPUC will execute any subgrant agreements if and when the CPUC and NTIA are able to resolve such disagreements and any other applicable conditions are met,” Reynolds wrote. “To that end, we will direct our staff to work diligently and cooperatively with NTIA staff to find such a solution.”

Whether California’s strategy works “depends on what happens next,” Stanford Law professor Barbara van Schewick, a longtime proponent of net neutrality and other telecom regulations, told Ars today.

“The letter doesn’t change the terms of California’s award: Condition 50 is still in it, and only a court or NTIA agreeing in writing can take it out,” she said. “The letter puts California’s position on the record before any contracts with providers are signed and preserves California’s legal arguments against Condition 50.”

Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office declined to comment when contacted by Ars today. A spokesperson for California Gov. Gavin Newsom said California is not giving up its right to enforce state laws against Internet providers.

“California is accepting federal broadband funding to bring high-speed Internet to hundreds of thousands of homes and businesses, many of them in rural and underserved communities,” a governor’s spokesperson said in a statement provided to Ars. “We’re ready to get these projects built with our local and federal partners. Connecting these communities is the goal, and so is protecting them. California’s laws, including our net neutrality protections, still stand.”

Net neutrality and throttling laws

California’s net neutrality law prohibits ISPs from blocking or throttling lawful traffic and says ISPs may not require fees from websites or online services to deliver or prioritize their traffic to Internet users. The first Trump administration lost an attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws, and California defeated ISPs that challenged the state law in court.

California also has a law that prohibits mobile providers from throttling first responders during emergencies. That law was passed in 2019 , a year after Verizon throttled an “unlimited” data plan used by Santa Clara County firefighters during a wildfire. Local wildfire-preparedness groups warned that the BEAD condition could prevent California from enforcing the throttling law and requirements for battery backups on cell towers.

According to van Schewick, “California has strong arguments that Condition 50 is illegal. Congress designed BEAD to get broadband built while making sure the providers who take the money follow the law: the statute directs states to ensure funded providers can carry out their work ‘in compliance with all applicable Federal, State, and local laws.’”

But van Schewick said the letter is just an initial step. “The real test comes the first time a BEAD provider blocks a competitor’s app, throttles firefighters, or walks away from a price commitment,” she said. “If the state enforces its laws when that happens, the letter will have protected Californians. If the state looks the other way, Condition 50 will have worked exactly as the providers intended, without a single court ever ruling on it.”

stories.title: What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?
stories.summary: The interest rate set by the Bank of England affects mortgage, loan and savings rates for millions.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 16 July 2021

Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to raise UK interest rates for the first time in more than three years at their next meeting.

Most analysts believe the Bank rate will go up from 3.75% to 4%, following holds at the previous six meetings.

Before the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February, rates had been expected to fall this year, but the economic fallout from the conflict has pushed up inflation across the globe.

Interest rates affect mortgage, credit card and savings rates for millions of people.

What are interest rates and why do they change?

An interest rate tells you how much it costs to borrow money, or the reward for saving it.

The Bank of England's base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what they charge their own customers for mortgages as well as the interest rate they pay on savings.

The Bank moves its base rate up and down in order to keep UK inflation — the rate at which prices are increasing — at or near 2%.

When inflation is above that target, the Bank typically puts rates up.

The idea is to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises.

What is happening to UK interest rates and inflation?

The Bank of England's base rate rose to 5.25% in August 2023. It remained at that level until August 2024, when the Bank started cutting.

Five cuts brought rates down to 4%, before the Bank held rates at its meetings in September and November 2025.

It then cut in December 2025 before holding rates steady in January, March, April, June, July and September 2026.

Meanwhile, the main UK inflation measure, CPI, has fallen significantly since the October 2022 high of 11.1%, which was caused by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

However, the rate has been heading back up and is expected to go higher. It was 3.5% in the year to September 2026 , up from 3.1% the previous month and well above the central bank's 2% target.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS), which tracks UK inflation, blamed the acceleration on sharp rises in petrol and diesel prices.

The US-Israel war with Iran has put up energy and fuel costs around the world, which has increased the pace of price rises more generally.

What is happening to UK prices? Published 21 October

What is expected to happen to UK interest rates?

At the start of the year, the Bank had been expected to cut interest rates twice in 2026, with the first drop predicted to come in March or April.

However, the increase in fuel prices and inflation after the outbreak of the conflict has upended all of this. Oil prices initially rose sharply as a result of disruption to supplies in the region, but dropped back when various ceasefires were agreed.

Oil prices rose again when the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July.

UK household energy bills rose after the increases in the price cap in July and October, while global oil prices have risen again recently.

Given the uncertainty, many analysts think UK interest rates will rise at the November meeting and again early next year.

What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills? Published 28 September

Why are UK fuel prices rising again? Published 2 October

How do interest rate changes affect mortgages, loans and savings rates?

Just under a third of households have a mortgage, according to the government's English Housing Survey , external .

About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate.

Any rise in the Bank rate means an increase in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. For a typical loan, the cost would go up by about £31 a month if the Bank raises the base rate by 0.25 percentage points, but it depends on the size of people's loans.

An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) would wait to see if their lender chose to pass on any Bank rate rise. Typically, this would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments for a 0.25 percentage points rates rise.

But the vast majority of mortgage customers - some 87% - have fixed-rate deals. While their monthly payments aren't immediately affected by a rate change, their future deals are.

Most lenders have already priced in a rise in the Bank rate in November, so this is already reflected in any rates being offered.

As of 4 November, the average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate was at 5.96%, while the average five-year rate stood at 5.99%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.

The average two-year tracker rate was 4.67%.

About 800,000 fixed-rate mortgages with an interest rate of 3% or below are expected to expire every year, on average, until the end of 2027. Borrowing costs for customers coming off those deals are likely to rise sharply.

Credit cards and loans

Bank of England interest rates also influence the amount charged on credit cards, new bank loans and car loans.

Lenders can decide to raise their own interest rates if Bank hikes make borrowing costs more expensive.

Equally, they can cut their own rates if Bank cuts make borrowing cheaper.

Savings

The Bank base rate also affects how much savers earn on their money.

A rising base rate is likely to mean an increase in the returns offered to savers by banks and building societies and vice versa.

As of 4 November, Moneyfacts said the average rate for an easy access savings account based on a balance of £10,000 was 2.58%. The average rate for an easy access cash ISA was 2.79%.

The average rate for customers who were prepared to lock their money away for a year was 4.48%.

Changes in rates particularly affect those who rely on the interest from their savings to top up their income.

What is happening to interest rates in other countries?

In recent years, the UK has had one of the highest interest rates in the G7 - the group representing the world's seven largest so-called "advanced" economies.

In June 2024, the European Central Bank (ECB) started cutting the main interest rate for the eurozone from an all-time high of 4%, falling to 2% in June 2025.

However, in June 2026, the ECB raised rates to 2.25% as it reacted to the Iran war, before raising them again to 2.5% in September.

The US central bank - the Federal Reserve - raised rates for the first time in three years at its September meeting , the third under the new chair Kevin Warsh.

It meant rates rose to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75%, following three cuts since September 2025.

US President Donald Trump had repeatedly attacked the previous Fed chair Jerome Powell for not cutting rates.

Warsh said the rise was because "inflation is too high and has been for too long", adding that it was a "sober" and "responsible decision".

After the announcement, Trump expressed support for Warsh but said the Fed board, which votes on rate decisions, was "hostile".

German carmaker slashes profit margin to between -0.5% and 0.5% this year in face of competition from China

The German carmaker BMW has issued its second profit warning in a year, blaming the costs of a restructuring programme including significant job losses in the face of continuing competition from China .

The company is the latest to issue a profit downgrade in the German car sector, with Mercedes-Benz last week cutting its profit outlook. Western automakers have struggled to keep pace with lower-cost domestic rivals in China, which has led to reduced sales there and a rise in exports to Europe .

BMW signalled a potential for losses after slashing its profit margin to between -0.5% and 0.5% this year but blamed fourth-quarter costs tied to the restructuring that includes 8,000 job cuts in its home market . At the beginning of the year, BMW had still considered a margin of 4-6% would be possible.

It reported an 11% drop in third-quarter pre-tax earnings on Wednesday to €2.1bn (£1.75bn).

Sales in China fell 22% in the first nine months of the year but BMW said this was in line with the broader downturn ⁠in that market.

“Current developments in our industry call for decisiveness and swift implementation. We will therefore specifically intensify and accelerate structural measures,” the chief executive Milan Nedeljković said.

China “remains a key focus”, Nedeljković added, with the group’s Neue Klasse ​revival of its model offering beginning in ​China this month with the launch of the iX3.

BMW follows Volkswagen with painful restructuring costs caused by the rapidly changing market.

Because of the rapid launch of its new generation of electric vehicles, the company is writing off parts of its previous vehicle and technology generations and pricing in the costs of the redundancy programme.

The operating ‌margin in BMW’s core ‌automotive business narrowed to 3.4%, beating analysts’ forecast of 3.1% but declining from 5.2% a year earlier.

Excluding restructuring charges, the margin would be above 2%, within its previous forecast range, the company said.

after newsletter promotion

BMW said it planned to cut management functions more quickly under its restructuring drive.

Revenue fell 6% to €30.4bn in the third quarter, hurt by the declining sales in China.

Although BMW’s ​rival Mercedes-Benz also reported lower profits in the third quarter, Porsche rebounded slightly but only after steep charges last year as it overhauls its model lineup and retreats from China.

stories.title: Children spending too long on maths app TT Rockstars, MP warns
stories.summary: The makers of the popular times table game say they are bringing in curfews and limits to screen time.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 34 minutes ago

Concerns have been raised with the government about the amount of time primary school children are spending on a game designed to make learning times tables fun.

TT Rockstars, which allows children to compete with their classmates for virtual coins and rock-star themed characters and outfits, is widely used by schools for maths homework.

Labour MP Emily Darlington said the app and others like it could be harming children's development because it rewards them for "length of time rather than quality of time spent online".

Bruno Reddy, founder of the firm behind TT Rockstars, said he shared concerns about screen time and was working with schools to bring in curfews and time limits.

He said the company discourages long sessions, adding: "Every game in TTRS is deliberately short, and our characters remind children to take regular breaks.

"The rule of thumb we give schools is: three minutes, four or five times a week. In September, a typical child played on three days, for about six minutes each time."

He said that from 24 November "every school will have a curfew and a daily time limit switched on, and leaderboards switched off as default".

Darlington told BBC News that while education technology, or EdTech, can have a place in the classroom "when gamification is used, children spend hours online to 'earn' the latest outfit".

"Parents are concerned that this causes conflict on time spent on devices and the pressure to perform against classmates," she added, and this could deter them from taking part in real life, rather than screen-based, activities.

The Milton Keynes Central MP raised concerns about TT Rockstars on Tuesday at the Commons Science Committee, which is investigating the impact of screen time and digital devices on children's brain development.

The company behind TT Rockstars, Maths Circle, says that the app and a similar programme for addition and subtraction, Numbots, is used in 17,000 schools and over 100,000 households.

Reddy, a former maths teacher, said TT Rockstars had been designed to "boost learning in the classroom: recognising progress, celebrating achievement and making learning enjoyable".

He added: "We've deliberately steered away from features designed to keep children playing, such as streaks, random rewards, chat messages, loot boxes or notifications.

"There's no advertising and schools pay the same subscription however much their students play, so we have no commercial reason to want children on screen for longer."

The government is in the process of drawing up guidelines for schools and parents on the amount of time five to 16-year-olds should spend on screens.

Former maths teacher Bruno Reddy launched TT Rockstars in 2010

At the committee, early years education minister Paul Waugh said: "Gamification isn't the way to learn.

"That's the propaganda they [EdTech companies] will give you but it is all about driving their screen time and their screen use. So it's profit driven."

He said there were "ways of making learning fun" that did not involve "competition with yourself or with someone else" and EdTech should be about supporting teachers and not replacing them.

It comes amid growing calls for the use of EdTech in the classroom to be limited.

Charlotte Ashton, co-founder of Generation Focus, which campaigns for smartphone-free schools, said: "Increasingly parents and teachers are saying no to Ed Tech because for the vast majority of digital 'learning tools' there's very little evidence they actually improve learning and growing evidence they can be harmful."

She added: "Not all tech is bad, but until we are confident that new digital tools improve children's learning without doing harm or imposing unintended consequences we are supporting schools to stick to proven teaching methods."

stories.title: Trump wanted to give No Kings no air. Then, Meta suspended its Instagram.
stories.summary: Meta faces pressure to protect No Kings Instagram on election day.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Meta faces pressure to protect No Kings Instagram on election day.

Over the weekend, the No Kings Coalition said Meta declined to commit to taking steps to prevent automated systems from suspending one of Instagram’s most prominent pro-democracy accounts if activity surged around the page during the midterm elections.

A demand for action came after Meta apologized for temporarily suspending the No Kings Instagram account and disabling access for four hours at the peak of an early voting push from the group. In a post on X, Meta’s Andy Stone said the account had been using a Claude AI tool in a way that made it appear to be a bot. But even though automated review detected the error within an hour, Stone acknowledged that additional hurdles kept admins locked out. State and federal lawmakers—as well as a coalition of 14 attorneys general —have asked Meta to further explain its actions.

In a letter to No Kings, Meta offered to arrange a meeting with a technical expert who could better explain the mistake. But No Kings rejected the response, saying it failed to address any of the group’s ongoing concerns and requesting a meeting with Meta senior leadership instead. The group stressed that the issue goes beyond its Instagram account, saying that Americans who rely on Meta’s platforms need assurance that voting content won’t be suppressed ahead of or on election day. Among eight questions, the coalition asked Meta to publicly disclose any communications with the Trump administration about the No Kings account or the historic early voting day event.

On October 30, Meta executives met with No Kings. According to the coalition’s account of the meeting, Meta said it has “no plans” to change policies that lead to harmful over-enforcement, a problem that even the independent Oversight Board , which reviews Meta’s content decisions, worries could result in suppression or censorship of No Kings and other pro-democracy content during this critical period.

“Meta acknowledged that it made a mistake, but an apology without action does nothing to ensure that this kind of censorship won’t happen again,” No Kings said, calling Meta’s laissez-faire attitude “unacceptable.”

Ars has found no evidence that the Trump administration asked Meta to restrict the No Kings account or that anyone at Meta intentionally targeted the account for political reasons. Meta told No Kings that it planned to post a public reply to the coalition’s demands, but the company did not respond to Ars’ request for comment, and Stone has yet to post an update on X. His account did, however, apologize for another accidental enforcement action impacting a Republican-controlled account the day before the No Kings meeting. “We automatically removed the @MOSenateGOP Facebook account because our systems mistakenly assessed the account was impersonating another one,” Stone said.

“This was never simply about a technical glitch or one Instagram account,” No Kings’ press release said. “It’s about whether millions of Americans can rely on these platforms to organize, communicate, and access critical voting information without disruption.”

Meta’s AI explanation seems incomplete

Formed in 2025 after Donald Trump returned to office for a second term, the No Kings Coalition is best known for organizing some of the largest coordinated protests in recent US history. Using social media channels to coordinate nationwide demonstrations against Trump policies viewed as anti-democratic, organizers estimated that more than 5 million people participated in its first protests in June 2025 and say attendance has only increased since. No Kings estimates 7 million people attended the second protests in October 2025, and more than 8 million showed up for the third demonstration last March.

For the fourth event, however, No Kings sought to get more than 9 million people into the streets, and then directly to the polls, by organizing an early voting event on October 17. Unlike the family-friendly protests where Americans held up signs demanding “No Kings in America,” this event focused on driving voter turnout. Although No Kings describes itself as a pro-democracy coalition with no interest in building up the Democratic Party, turnout for its events is driven by those who oppose Trump’s most controversial policies—including domestic ICE enforcement and US military involvement in Iran.

Hundreds of civil rights organizations, including Black Voters Matter and the American Civil Liberties Union, make up the No Kings Coalition. Initially, there was no centralized Instagram account where the groups could coordinate their social media messaging. But as the November 3 election approached, the coalition got more organized, hoping that an official No Kings account with a large following would help it identify and amplify content ahead of the fourth event.

That’s when No Kings decided to use Claude as a “keyword and hashtag search tool to track conversations across social media platforms,” the group’s social media team told Ars.

According to Stone, the Claude tool was “reading profiles, posts, and hashtags,” which “sharply” increased the account’s activity in “intense bursts” that “resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems.”

Ars could not determine what specific Claude-powered tool the coalition was using, how it accessed Instagram, or whether it was an Anthropic service or a third-party integration built using Claude. Ars asked both Anthropic and Meta whether there was anything unusual about the way No Kings was using Claude, but neither company responded.

Ezra Levin, co-founder of Indivisible, a progressive nonprofit in the No Kings Coalition, told Ars that the volume of posting increases because organizers understand a basic principle of advertising: “You’ve got to reach people seven different times in seven different ways, and it’s the seventh time that they hear, and they’re like, ‘Oh right, there is an early vote action going on. I should get out there.’”

The high volume shouldn’t matter, though, Levin said, emphasizing that “it seems pretty absurd that a social media company that doesn’t go down during the Super Bowl or during the World Series or during the Oscars shuts our account down during an early vote push.”

“We’re not using any boutique tools that nobody has developed before,” Levin said. “These are all nonprofits. We’re putting things together with popsicle sticks and glue. We’re not developing our own sophisticated apparatus. So there is nothing that I’m aware of that is unique about how we were using the social media platform that day.”

Meta’s closer ties with Trump fuel suspicion

Levin pointed to a series of episodes dating back to at least 2016 that raised questions about Meta’s role in protecting democratic processes. That year, Facebook acknowledged that it sold election-related ads to a shadowy Russian company . More recently, Meta faced questions from Congress in 2021 after turning off election-related safeguards and failing to detect “Stop the Steal” groups from gaming its algorithm to spread disinformation. After Trump’s 2024 election and shortly before his inauguration, Meta announced that it would end its US third-party fact-checking program. Zuckerberg also said Meta would work with Trump to push back against what he characterized as censorship by foreign governments. Critics warned that the move amounted to Meta declaring that “the truth doesn’t matter .”

To Levin, Meta’s playbook for handling controversies like the No Kings Instagram suspension is to lawyer up, offer technical explanations, and issue “empty apologies.”

Levin also pointed to Meta’s decision to donate $1 million to Trump’s inaugural fund and later $5 million for Trump’s ballroom project , which Levin said were blatant efforts to curry favor with the president.

Given what Levin sees as Zuckerberg’s alignment with Trump, he said it’s difficult for No Kings to accept that a technical glitch, rather than deliberate action by someone at Meta, was behind the suspension. Levin acknowledged that some posts that appear to be suppressed on Meta platforms may simply fail to get traction. But given Meta’s history with election content and its failure to make changes to protect pro-democracy content, he said, it’s difficult for outsiders to not be skeptical.

For example, Levin said Meta never acknowledged that at least one No Kings creator’s account was also suspended on the day the No Kings account was disabled. Other No Kings creators have reported that some Instagram posts seemingly receive no views.

“This is why the history does matter,” Levin said. “The context matters here because if I believed Meta to be a corporation that was operating above-board and was stridently pro-democracy and always erred in the defense of people organizing, I would say, ‘Look, it’s Meta. You know Meta, they wouldn’t do that. Probably there’s something else going on.’ But you would have to not have your head screwed on straight to believe that based on the publicly available information.”

Trump seems to shift No Kings tactics

Levin told Ars that one of his biggest remaining questions is whether Meta had any interactions with the Trump administration ahead of the suspension.

To No Kings, the Trump administration had been vocal in its opposition to the protests during the coalition’s first two events. Last October, Trump controversially posted an AI-generated video of a jet labeled “King Trump” flying over protesters while blasting the Kenny Loggins song “Danger Zone.” He has also directly dismissed protesters as an “ineffective” “joke,” echoing comments from others in his administration.

But Trump may have realized that such comments were only drawing more attention to the movement, and there has since been a “notable tactical shift,” Levin suggested. Trump and his supporters now seem to pointedly refuse to discuss No Kings, perhaps hoping to deny the movement oxygen, he said.

“It’s not absurd to think they were also talking to their friends in social media and asking them to not cover this as much or tilt the algorithm a certain way,” Levin said.

Although four hours may not seem like a long time, any disruption that makes it harder for No Kings to reach people has a significant impact, Levin said.

“We are forced to use these platforms that are privately owned in order to reach these folks,” Levin said. “And in using the platforms, we are vulnerable to this kind of pressure, and that directly undermines our ability to reach these people.”

If the same thing happened “in the middle of election day, where pro-democracy accounts are suppressed or shut down,” that could be “cataclysmic,” Levin said.

Lawmakers, AGs probe Meta

David Greene, senior counsel for the digital rights group the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), told Ars that the timing of the No Kings Instagram suspension is “suspicious” and that Meta’s technical excuse is “a really incomplete answer.”

As No Kings continues to demand that Meta release any communications with Trump, Meta also faces increased pressure from lawmakers and state officials to make changes to support accounts like No Kings during election day.

Last week, a coalition of 14 state attorneys general sent a letter to Meta demanding a more transparent explanation of the suspension. By October 29, they asked Meta to “detail its plans to ensure that legitimate election activity on Meta platforms is not disrupted.”

“This is particularly concerning given the proliferation of AI agents marketed to consumers, including by Meta, as compatible with social media accounts,” the attorneys general wrote.

Ars could not confirm whether the coalition’s deadline was met, but the attorneys general weren’t alone in expressing concern that Meta may be “unable to differentiate between legitimate political activity and bot activity that harms users” in the age of AI.

Democratic Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen sent a similar request, The New Republic reported , specifically asking why it took so long for Meta to help admins regain access. In Congress, Robert Garcia and Jamie Raskin, members of the House Oversight Committee and House Judiciary Committee, also probed Meta for answers. Levin noted that these lawmakers could become future chairs of those committees if the elections swing No Kings’ way.

In Levin’s ideal world, “the next Congress” would “take a very different approach” to regulating the tech industry. He believes that could have significant consequences ahead of the next presidential election. Rather than seeing tech CEOs aligned with the executive branch, there could finally be a more “healthy” public debate, where “different presidential candidates” may adopt “different positions of their orientation towards Silicon Valley,” Levin said.

The path Meta is not taking

Greene suggested that Meta could take steps such as requiring human review of election-related content or creating emergency support channels to quickly address automated throttling, inadvertent suspensions, or content removals.

Although Meta has no legal obligation to do so, Greene said, “they certainly have an obligation to their users to anticipate these things and to be ready for them.”

Greene told Ars that he agreed with Meta’s Oversight Board, which directed Meta to take proactive steps to protect election-related content rather than simply waiting to fix problems after an account is automatically suspended. One possible solution, Greene suggested, would be a notification system allowing No Kings to notify Meta when major events are planned so the company can prepare.

“Clearly if it was a technical problem, it’s a technical problem that should have been expected and thought about ahead of time and anticipated and addressed ahead of time,” Greene said. “The No Kings stuff was not secret in any way.”

Like Levin, Greene pointed to Meta’s history of mishandling election content, not just in the US but around the world. Levin noted that No Kings worked with election organizers in Brazil, where Meta also recently faced allegations of electoral interference .

“These are technical glitches that happen around elections all the time, and Meta just needs to have an affirmative plan for this and not just try to respond as they happen,” Greene said. “And I think until they do that, they’re not going to dispel suspicion that things are politically motivated.”

The EFF believes the Trump administration should disclose all its communications with Meta, but so far neither side is clarifying whether Trump may be influencing how Meta handles election-related content, Greene said.

Greene said it’s difficult to determine whether Meta was engaged in “jawboning,” with the Trump administration pressuring the platform to silence dissidents. However, “the explanation they’ve given is so inadequate that it’s hard to discount the [idea] that there was political influence,” he said.

And he agreed that a four-hour admin lockout was too long.

“Because as we know, when you’re organizing a protest, even if you shorten this to a three-minute delay from a three-hour delay, that could be consequential,” Greene said. “And so, the idea is to avoid these things in the first place.”

Kate Ruane, director of the Center for Democracy and Technology’s Free Expression Project, told Ars that Meta must explain not only why its automated systems flagged accounts like the No Kings Instagram account but also why the “mistake prevention systems” it designed to avoid such situations “were not triggered in this circumstance.”

Ruane noted that the CDT supports the JAWBONE Act , which “would require the government to be transparent with the public about communications from the government to online speech intermediaries related to the constitutionally protected speech they distribute.” If the next Congress passes that law, Meta could face greater scrutiny if questions about the No Kings suspension remain unanswered. Levin suggested that “a pro-democracy Congress” would send subpoenas, hold hearings, and use legislative processes to hold Meta accountable.

“Large-scale political speech events are frequently organized using Meta’s services,” Ruane said. “It is critical for users engaged in those activities to understand exactly what happened and how they and Meta can avoid it in the future.”

stories.body:
The U.S. Postal Service used social media surveillance to monitor and report on protests across the political spectrum, government records show.

The records , disclosed to EFF and other requesters suing the postal service under the Freedom of Information Act, show that the agency’s internet Covert Operations Program, or iCOP, routinely sifted through social media posts organizing and discussing protests with little records of any oversight or legal justification.

EFF filed suit in 2021 after Yahoo News disclosed the program’s existence and how the agency used it to monitor First Amendment protected activities. After years of delays and technical failures that led the agency to lose access to a trove of emails discussing the program, the postal service disclosed records to EFF and several other requesters this year.

The Postal Service used iCOP to surveil First Amendment activities

The disclosures include a series of bulletins created from iCOP, which show that the postal service used the program in 2020 and 2021 to monitor and circulate information about a wide range of planned protests. They included a planned “ Million MAGA March ,” a guns rights advocacy event and counter-protest in Virginia, a nationwide Save the Post Office Saturday protest , and planned protests in front of then-Postmaster General Louis DeJoy’s home in Washington, D.C.

Many of the bulletins provide dry descriptions of the events being planned and reference public discussions or events on major social media services. Others seem to imply or anticipate that the protests would turn violent.

For example, in discussing planned national and international protests scheduled for March 20, 2021 , the bulletin references potential violence in light of “online inflammatory material.” Yet the bulletin acknowledges that the agency has “no intelligence to suggest specific threats.” This bulletin was described by Yahoo News when it disclosed iCOP’s existence.

Another bulletin discussing an ongoing Black Lives Matter protests in response to police shooting and killing people styles itself as a “ National Civil Unrest Update. ” The bulletins also recount and monitor threats sent to then-Postmaster DeJoy.

The Postal Service also disclosed three email chains to EFF that, while heavily redacted, show how the agency queried iCOP and disseminated what it found (Read the emails here , here , and here ). The government agreed to release the email messages as part of settling EFF’s FOIA suit this fall. To EFF’s knowledge, they are the only existing materials that reflect how the agency queried iCOP.

Postal Service renames iCOP and loses access to records about it

According to the agency, after Yahoo News disclosed the program in 2021, the postal service renamed it and publicly said that it had stopped issuing bulletins . But the documents do not say that the agency’s social media surveillance stopped.

At the same time, EFF and several other FOIA requesters sought records detailing how the agency used iCOP and what rules the postal service had for using the program and distributing information it gained from surveilling social media. EFF spent years pushing the agency to disclose email communications about the program, which the agency had stored on an external hard drive. Amid these negotiations, someone dropped the hard drive, rendering it inoperable, agency officials said . By the time that happened, the agency had already deleted the underlying email messages pursuant to the agency’s retention schedule.

Minimal records disclosed about internal limits on surveillance programs

EFF’s FOIA request sought internal rules, guidance, and training that would show what safeguard the Postal Service imposed to protect First Amendment rights. The agency disclosed very few documents in response to this part of EFF’s request.

For example, a series of slides give an overview of the program, but do not explain how officials used iCOP. The closest thing to internal guideline that the agency disclosed were talking points the Chief Postal Inspector authored in response to questions about iCOP.

The inspector wrote that, “In reviewing social media postings to gather information we did not single out any particular group and did not base what was reviewed on race, religion, gender, sexual orientation, immigration status, or a person’s exercise of First Amendment freedoms.” The statement echoes language in the bulletin stating that its purpose is not to infringe on First Amendment rights; Other parts of the talking points characterize the surveillance as providing officials with situational awareness.

The postal inspector’s talking points go on to say that “the recent attention on iCOP has highlighted opportunities for improvement, including enhanced executive oversight. We have stopped the distribution of the bulletins like the one you have seen in the media reports.”

Setting aside that it’s unclear whether internal oversight occurred or resulted in any changes, the claim that iCOP did not infringe on First Amendment rights rings hollow. As the records disclosed show, surveilling and reporting on social media users’ efforts to organize rallies and protests was a feature of iCOP.

But more fundamentally, the claims by Postal Service officials fail to recognize that surveillance directly chills First Amendment rights. Further, the government can misuse the information it obtained as part of its social media surveillance to harass or retaliate against those exercising their constitutional rights.

Although EFF’s case seeking records about iCOP has ended, we will continue to bring more transparency to the government’s use of social media surveillance and look for ways to challenge the practice, especially when people are caught in the dragnet for exercising the First Amendment rights.

stories.title: Miliband says slavery apology will not bring cost for UK taxpayers
stories.summary: Speaking to BBC's Newscast, the foreign secretary says Britain cannot sweep its past "under the carpet".

stories.body:
Ed Miliband tells the BBC's Newscast podcast it is "right to confront this issue" of the transatlantic slavery trade

Published 9 hours ago

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has insisted the government's willingness to consider formally apologising for the UK's role in the transatlantic slave trade will not lead to higher costs for the British taxpayer.

The prime minister has said the UK will not pay reparations to affected countries, but declined to say whether his new approach could involve additional taxpayer money.

Speaking on the BBC's Newscast podcast, Miliband said previous British governments had a "sweep it under the carpet" attitude to the pain and consequences of slavery, citing what he described as former Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair's "sorry not sorry" remarks on the issue nearly two decades ago.

In 2007, Sir Tony said the UK's involvement in the slave trade was a matter of "deep sorrow and regret".

"Tony Blair did sort of do a kind of sorry not sorry situation. He kind of expressed sorrow, and then said sorry, and then it was walked back by number 10," Miliband said.

Miliband said the former prime minister's approach was still referred to and came up in a recent conversation between Andy Burnham and the Prime Minister of Barbados Mia Mottley.

In addition, Miliband claimed, he and Burnham inherited a more recent mess, which is how the last Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) played out in Samoa two years ago.

Miliband said: "On the second day as my time as foreign secretary, I was told, 'look, one of your tasks is CHOGM 2024, which happened in Samoa, didn't go well.' To use sort of diplomatic speak, it ended up in a sort of punch up, a sort of verbal punch up about this whole issue."

He added: "This has really been hanging around as an issue for the Commonwealth for sort of 20 years, really. But it's grown and grown."

Given that, Miliband said, "we thought it was right to confront this issue and not to just try and sort of pretend that it didn't exist".

King calls slave trade a 'shameful chapter' during Commonwealth address Published 15 hours ago

PM plans debt reset for Commonwealth nations as slavery apology talks begin Published 1 day ago

Burnham now says the government is open to formally apologising for slavery.

Ministers are beginning what they call a "structured dialogue" with affected countries, with the expectation that the apology may come at around the time the prime minister hosts the G20 Summit of world leaders in Manchester in November 2027.

"Is it weak to do this? I think it's the opposite of weak. I think fragile weak countries can't face up to their past. I'm really proud of Britain, but being proud of your country is also being willing to face up to things you didn't do, right?" Miliband said.

He said he had asked to be provided with a historical digest of the UK's involvement in the slave trade.

"Over three million people shipped, really with the British state's complicity, over a long period of time, couple of centuries actually, hundreds of thousands of them didn't make it and died," the foreign secretary said.

"Those who did make it had appalling conditions. Reading about the conditions on the ships and what happened to them when they arrived in the Caribbean and the Americas is really pretty harrowing."

Now he and the prime minister begin a process likely to formally apologise for this -and, they hope, create space for the Commonwealth to turn its attention to other things.

stories.summary: The government’s surveillance powers grew rapidly after Sept. 11, 2001, some in public view and some in secret. EFF suspected but couldn’t prove that the National Security Agency was spying on Americans' communications. The New York Times sat on a story about it for over a year, finally publishing it in December 2005. Then, in January 2006, a retired AT&T technician named Mark Klein walked into EFF's office with a manila folder of documents that blew the story wide open. To pass the time, I started chatting to a stranger. He had an easy, confident way of speaking, which I admired. We discussed topics I know little about: the instability of modern economies, the feasibility of commercial space travel, the likelihood of a coup in Russia. I found myself leaning in and asking questions: I felt as if I could learn a lot from this person. We eventually got to psychology, which is more my wheelhouse. I brooded about how easy it’s become for people to accept strange ideas. “Some people will believe anything,” he observed. “Some people even believe the Earth is round !” It’s increasingly difficult to ignore how fragmented and bizarre our beliefs have become. Concern over greater AI regulation, while investors move into US treasuries as Trump faces political gridlock

Business live – latest updates

US midterm elections – live updates

The US dollar has fallen sharply after the Democrats won control of the Senate and the House in the midterm elections, sparking fears that greater regulation of AI could slow economic growth.

The dollar hit a one-month low on Wednesday while coming under pressure from falling bond yields, as investors moved into US treasuries, viewed as a safe haven from the political gridlock anticipated during the rest of Donald Trump’s final term in office.

The dollar index, which measures it against a basket of six currencies, slid to its lowest level in a month and the pound and the euro gained against the dollar. The US currency also slid against the yen and the Swiss franc, currencies that traders tend to turn to during times of uncertainty.

Meanwhile, the yield, or interest rate, on the benchmark 10-year US treasury bond has fallen 4.7 basis points to 4.918%, while the two-year bond yield has dropped 3.7bps to 4.597%. Yields fall when bond prices rise.

American voters rejected Trump and the Republican party’s agenda across the country, as the Democrats’ “blue wave” led to the party securing Senate seats in traditional Republican strongholds such as Texas, Iowa, North Carolina and South Carolina.

Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the trading platform IG, said: “The scale of the losses will inevitably raise questions about Trump’s ability to push through his agenda over the next two years, and markets are already reacting. The dollar is under pressure as investors reassess the political outlook, while gold and silver are benefiting as safe haven plays.”

Futures trading initially indicated US stock markets would open sharply lower, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq expected to slide on fears over the prospects for AI companies. However, indicators later suggested Wall Street could open higher as Trump’s conciliatory tone and rises on European markets cheered investors.

European markets climbed in early trading, with a 0.2% rise on London’s FTSE 100, while Germany’s Dax climbed by almost 0.6%, France’s Cac 40 was 0.4% up and Italy’s FTSE MiB index jumped by almost 1.4%.

Bank and clean energy stocks, which have borne the brunt of Donald Trump’s policies, were among the top risers in Europe. Bank stocks rose by 2.8%, while Denmark’s Vestas Wind Systems jumped nearly 5% and Ørsted soared 7.4%.

“Some individual names are nursing significant losses today,” said Kathleen Brooks, the research director UK at XTB. “SpaceX is down 5% in the premarket, and Tesla is lower by more than 4%. Elon Musk is considered an anathema to most Democrats .”

Musk, the world’s richest person, pumped $446m (£331m) into the midterms , funding Republican-aligned political action committees and groups.

Brooks said investors were reacting to expectations that a Democrat-controlled Congress could mean greater scrutiny for AI companies, which could also cast doubt on a potential merger between Musk’s two companies.

stories.body:
The latest edition of Radical Thinking, the Guardian’s new podcast, should be required listening at a Treasury still stifled by outdated orthodoxies

A s prime ministers have come and gone at bewildering speed in recent years, the search for elusive economic growth has become the overriding fixation of the British political class. In the lead-up to the 2024 general election, Sir Keir Starmer declared that “growth must become Labour’s obsession”, given the financial constraints that any new government would be under. The scale of Labour’s progressive offer, it was made clear, would be umbilically linked to its ability to generate a significant uptick in GDP.

“Growth in every postcode” is also the early mantra of Andy Burnham’s government. The prime minister swept to power partly by running on Greater Manchester’s record as the UK’s fastest-growing city region while he was mayor. Echoing Mr Starmer’s approach, Mr Burnham’s chancellor, John Healey, told the Labour party conference in September: “Without growth, there is no social democracy.”

But as the economists Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal suggest in the latest edition of the Guardian’s new Radical Thinking podcast, that is a flawed and politically unhelpful linkage to make. In a transformed geopolitical environment, they argue, the notion that former levels of growth can be restored is likely to prove a chimera. Just as importantly – as the contrast between Manchester’s booming city centre and hard-pressed towns such as Oldham and Wigan illustrates – better growth rates would not solve entrenched problems of affordability in places unlikely ever to become hubs for advanced manufacturing or financial services.

Yet neither of those assertions mean that an ambitious egalitarian politics must be ruled out. “We need to say: ‘How do low-income places work?’,” Prof Williams says. “What do we need to do to get them to work better?” Or as Prof Johal puts it: “What are the basics, the necessities that we need … for people to have a decent civilised life?” At the most fundamental level, a more ambitiously redistributive fiscal approach can bring bills down for the less well-off. More broadly, shifting resources into the essential building blocks of every local community – transport, utilities, care networks and other social and physical infrastructure – can improve everyday lives by restoring collective control over public goods.

Mr Burnham’s signature move as mayor – the decision to take Greater Manchester’s buses back under public control and cap fares – suggests a shared agenda here. But the prime minister has sent mixed messages when it comes to “ Manchesterism ” – the place-based economic strategy that he wishes to export to the nation. As the role of the United Arab Emirates in the city’s modern development comes under scrutiny, Mr Burnham’s version of “ business-friendly socialism ” is a political philosophy in need of greater definition. Devolution should involve funnelling local power downwards and outwards, rather than upwards to Abu Dhabi-type investors in the indiscriminate pursuit of growth.

A greater focus on the “ foundational ” economy described by Prof Williams and Prof Johal can help with that project. One of Mr Burnham’s last acts as mayor was to sign off on a mayoral development corporation for the town of Middleton , near Manchester. Its agenda is being shaped by residents and local business owners, with the aspiration that local economic networks can be “rewired” and the provision of everyday essentials be reconfigured and improved. Given proper backing from Westminster, social democrats do not need to wait for growth before they can begin improving lives.

stories.body:
De nouvelles sanctions sont imposées dans la région des Grands Lacs. Alors que le Burundi est désormais épargné , son voisin du nord, le Rwanda, est à son tour visé.

Washington vient en effet de sanctionner le ministère rwandais de la Défense, en raison de son implication dans le conflit en République démocratique du Congo (RDC).

Les précédentes sanctions avaient été annoncées le 2 mars 2026, date à laquelle l’armée rwandaise avait elle aussi été visée.

Le département d’État américain justifie ces mesures par la volonté de faire respecter les accords de Washington signés le 4 décembre 2025, qui visent à mettre fin au conflit en RDC, ainsi qu’à développer le commerce et les investissements dans la région.

Mes recherches doctorales portent sur les sanctions internationales, notamment celles adoptées par l’Union européenne et des organisations régionales, ainsi que sur la résilience autoritaire dans les États fragiles, à travers une étude comparative axée sur le Burundi. J’y consacre également un chapitre à d’autres pays ayant fait l’objet de sanctions, notamment le Mali et le Niger. Dans cette perspective, les sanctions américaines imposées au Rwanda méritent elles aussi une attention particulière.

Les accords de Washington dans l’impasse

Ces accords reposent sur des engagements mutuels. Kigali doit cesser de soutenir les rebelles du Mouvement du 23 mars (M23) et retirer ses troupes du territoire congolais. De son côté, Kinshasa est tenu de neutraliser les Forces démocratiques de libération du Rwanda (FDLR) , un groupe armé né dans le sillage du génocide des Tutsi au Rwanda en 1994, et de faciliter leur retour au Rwanda.

Sur le terrain, presque rien ne bouge. La RDC a présenté un cadre qui, selon le gouvernement de Kinshasa, permettrait de désarmer les FDLR, notamment grâce à la signature d’un protocole d’accord avec ce groupe. Toutefois, une question demeure : comment ce processus sera-t-il concrètement mis en œuvre sur le plan opérationnel ?

À ce jour, aucune réponse claire n’a été apportée. Le Rwanda considère cette démarche comme une manœuvre dilatoire et continue de soutenir le M23) , un groupe rebelle, et de déployer des troupes en RDC. Les accords semblent ainsi au point mort.

Chacun des partis s’accuse mutuellement pour justifier ses actions. Cependant, les sanctions frappent continuellement une seule partie.

Read more: Burundi–Mali : comment les régimes autoritaires se maintiennent au pouvoir par la fabrique de l’ennemi

La sélectivité des sanctions : une pression à sens unique

De nombreuses études montrent que les sanctions tendent à être appliquées prioritairement dans les situations où les États « sanctionneurs » ont peu à perdre — notamment lorsqu'elles visent des pays fortement dépendants de l'aide internationale .

Les États les plus vulnérables d'Afrique subsaharienne sont aussi ceux qui subissent le plus fréquemment des mesures coercitives, tandis que d'autres échappent aux sanctions malgré des violations avérées des normes démocratiques.

Ici, il faut nuancer notre propos car les États-Unis ont aussi sanctionné des États comme la Russie, l’Iran ou le Venezuela, des pays qui ont maintenu leurs positions face aux pressions américaines. Dans le cas présent, l’asymétrie est d’autant plus frappante que la RDC dispose d’importantes ressources minières et se montre très disposée à coopérer avec les États-Unis.

Le Rwanda, dont le poids économique est très inférieur à celui de son voisin, dispose quant à lui de marges de manœuvre très réduites face à l’administration Trump.

La perversité des sanctions

La littérature académique a régulièrement mis en évidence les effets pervers des sanctions, qui atteignent rarement les objectifs initialement escomptés. Une étude estime leur taux de réussite à 34 % .

Ce chiffre est contesté par Robert Anthony Pape , politologue américain connu pour ses travaux sur les sanctions économiques et la coercition, qui estime leur taux de réussite à environ 4 %. Plusieurs cas montrent par ailleurs que les sanctions peuvent devenir un instrument de consolidation de l’autoritarisme.

Read more: Paix contre extraction en RDC : les limites de l’approche Trump

Les exemples récents ne manquent pas. L’Iran, soumis à des sanctions depuis des décennies, n’a pas vu son régime s’effondrer .

Au Venezuela, des années de sanctions n’ont pas provoqué l’alternance démocratique sous la présidence de Nicolás Maduro . En Afrique, l’Alliance des États du Sahel (AES) également sanctionnée, s’est tournée vers de nouveaux partenaires, tandis que le Burundi a traversé des années de sanctions occidentales sans changement politique.

Lorsque les sanctions échouent à atteindre leurs objectifs, faut-il pour autant recourir à l’intervention militaire ? Les exemples de la Libye et de l’Irak révèlent les conséquences de telles interventions et les difficultés qu’elles ont engendrées à l’échelle régionale.

En s’inscrivant dans une logique similaire à celle de la France sous la présidence de Nicolas Sarkozy , les États-Unis risquent à leur tour d’affaiblir leur crédibilité diplomatique à l’avenir, si ce n'est déjà fait.

Qu’en est-il de la région des Grands Lacs ?

S’agissant du Rwanda, la question des FDLR est existentielle. Le régime de Paul Kagame a lui-même été confronté à cette menace avant son arrivée au pouvoir et connaît les implications sécuritaires qu’elle soulève.

Quelles que soient les motivations de Kigali, les autorités rwandaises considèrent la présence de ce mouvement, issu de milieux liés aux auteurs du génocide, comme une menace directe pour le régime. Les sanctions à répétition risquent de renforcer une posture selon laquelle le pays doit compter sur ses propres moyens au nom de sa souveraineté.

Du côté de Kinshasa, le président Félix Tshisekedi est soupçonné de vouloir briguer un nouveau mandat et de modifier la Constitution. Les États-Unis semblent ainsi s’éloigner davantage des principes démocratiques en soutenant un pouvoir dont la trajectoire pourrait basculer vers l’autoritarisme. Pour Trump, l’autoritarisme ne semble pas constituer un problème, pourvu que ce pouvoir serve les intérêts des États-Unis.

La pression exercée sur Kigali, sans exigence comparable concernant la neutralisation des FDLR en RDC ni le respect des libertés politiques, n’incite guère Kinshasa à engager des réformes dans ces domaines. Elle risque, au contraire, d’encourager les autorités congolaises à poursuivre leurs propres ambitions.

L’administration Trump ne fait que mettre au grand jour une logique selon laquelle les sanctions servent les intérêts des puissances, une réalité jusque-là souvent moins ouvertement assumée. Les autres États observent cette évolution dans un monde où la loi du plus fort tend à s’imposer comme la règle. Une telle logique risque toutefois de produire un effet boomerang et de se retourner contre ceux-là mêmes qui prétendent en tirer profit.

stories.body:
Partout dans le monde, les populations ont directement ressenti les effets du changement climatique. L’hémisphère nord a connu un nouvel été record, marqué par des vagues de chaleur et des phénomènes météorologiques extrêmes .

L’hémisphère sud est désormais confronté à un été marqué par des vagues de chaleur, des inondations, des feux de forêt et des sécheresses. Cette situation s’inscrit dans un contexte de changement climatique installé depuis plusieurs décennies. Elle est aujourd’hui amplifiée par un épisode El Niño , phénomène climatique naturel marqué par un réchauffement périodique des eaux de surface dans le centre et l’est du Pacifique équatorial, associé à des variations des vents et de la circulation atmosphérique.

Des phénomènes météorologiques extrêmes liés au changement climatique ont contraint des communautés entières à se déplacer à la suite des récents cyclones et épisodes d’inondations au Népal . Les incendies de forêt qui ont frappé la France et l’Espagne en juillet 2026 ont contraint plus de 250 000 personnes à évacuer leur domicile ou leur lieu de séjour.

Plus de 250 000 personnes ont tout perdu lors d’un récent incendie de forêt en Espagne .

Dans les villes européennes, plus de 50 000 décès liés aux fortes chaleurs auraient été enregistrés au cours de l’été 2026. Selon une étude publiée dans la revue Nature Health, environ 65 % de ces décès seraient attribuables au changement climatique d’origine humaine. Ces chiffres rappellent que le changement climatique n’est pas une simple menace pour l’avenir : il constitue déjà un danger immédiat pour les populations, en particulier les communautés et les personnes les plus vulnérables.

En tant que chercheurs et professionnels de la santé publique cherchant à comprendre et à répondre aux impacts sanitaires du changement climatique, cela nous préoccupe grandement. Dans nos propres travaux consacrés à l’impact de la chaleur sur les femmes enceintes et les enfants en Afrique, nous avons mis en évidence des conséquences profondes sur la santé de la mère pendant la grossesse, sur les complications à la naissance et sur des problèmes pouvant perdurer toute la vie chez les enfants à naître.

Dans une étude antérieure, nous avons également constaté que les professionnels de santé chargés de prendre en charge ces communautés vulnérables subissaient les effets négatifs du changement climatique.

Read more: Le changement climatique impacte la santé au Sénégal : voici comment y remédier

Plus récemment, nous avons mené , dans le cadre d’une recherche menée auprès de communautés en Afrique du Sud, des travaux visant à comprendre comment les populations tentent de s’adapter au changement climatique. Il apparaît de plus en plus clairement que les communautés ont conscience des risques auxquels elles sont confrontées en raison du changement climatique. Elles en font l’expérience au quotidien. Elles ne disposent tout simplement pas des ressources nécessaires pour s’adapter à ces changements.

L’Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS) et d’éminents scientifiques considèrent depuis des décennies le changement climatique comme l'une des plus grandes menaces pour la santé au XXIe siècle. Cependant, au lieu de mettre en place une architecture sanitaire mondiale capable d'anticiper et de répondre au changement climatique, nous, en tant que professionnels de la santé publique, avons laissé cette responsabilité à un système des Nations unies fondé sur le consensus .

Les progrès ont été désespérément lents et, plus récemment, le processus s’est complètement enlisé . Malgré les engagements successifs, le monde n’est pas parvenu à limiter le réchauffement climatique à 1,5 °C .

C’est dans cette optique que nous appelons l’OMS à déclarer que les impacts du changement climatique sur la santé constituent une urgence de santé publique de portée internationale . Cette déclaration permettrait de renforcer la volonté politique, de mobiliser des financements et de fournir des recommandations fondées sur des données probantes en vue d’une réponse urgente en matière de santé publique.

Impacts du changement climatique sur la santé

Les impacts du changement climatique sur la santé sont généralisés et aggravent la vulnérabilité des individus et des systèmes de santé. Les personnes âgées, les femmes enceintes, les enfants et les personnes atteintes de maladies chroniques sont les plus exposés à ces impacts. Or, ces populations sont souvent celles qui disposent du moins de ressources pour s’adapter. Les pays du Sud sont également parmi les plus durement touchés par le changement climatique, alors qu’ils comptent parmi les moins responsables des émissions qui le provoquent.

Pour ces populations, le changement climatique se traduit par de nouvelles mauvaises récoltes, qui exposent leurs enfants à la malnutrition . Les inondations peuvent aussi les couper de leur centre de santé et des médicaments dont ils ont besoin. Une saison de transmission du paludisme peut leur faire perdre un enfant ou un proche, victime d’une maladie évitable.

De plus, une vague de chaleur peut transformer une grossesse en épreuve douloureuse et mettre en danger la vie de la mère et de l’enfant.

De nouvelles méthodes scientifiques, comme l’attribution des effets du changement climatique sur la santé, sont développées pour mesurer précisément la part du changement climatique dans les effets observés sur la santé. Ces travaux contribuent à renforcer la confiance dans les résultats scientifiques.

Une marge de manœuvre réduite pour réagir alors qu’El Niño s’intensifie

Le monde est aujourd’hui confronté à une saison El Niño sans précédent. Un rapport récent prévoit 451 000 décès supplémentaires liés à la chaleur entre juin 2026 et février 2027. Ce chiffre équivaut à peu près au nombre de décès dus à la Covid-19 au cours des six premiers mois de la pandémie.

L’OMS dispose d’un mécanisme pour faire face aux menaces sans précédent pour la santé publique, en particulier celles qui nécessitent une collaboration internationale. Le Règlement sanitaire international définit très clairement les procédures et les mesures à prendre en réponse en cas d'urgence de santé publique de portée internationale. Celle-ci est définie comme :

un événement extraordinaire dont il est déterminé qu’il constitue un risque pour la santé publique dans d’autres États en raison du risque de propagation internationale de maladies et qu’il peut requérir une action internationale coordonnée.

Pour qu’une éventuelle urgence de santé publique de portée internationale soit déclenchée, le Règlement sanitaire international prescrit que deux des quatre conditions suivantes soient remplies :

La menace pour la santé publique est-elle grave ?

L’événement est-il inhabituel ou inattendu ?

Existe-t-il un risque significatif de propagation internationale ?

Existe-t-il un risque de restrictions en matière de voyages ou de commerce international ?

Appel à l’action

Nombreux sont ceux qui ont appelé à une telle déclaration en réponse à la crise climatique, qui remplit la plupart, voire la totalité, des critères. Nous avons fait valoir par ailleurs que tout retard supplémentaire entraînera des pertes humaines inutiles et causera des préjudices évitables aux plus vulnérables de la société.

Cet appel urgent a été soutenu par les ministères de la Santé de plusieurs pays d’Afrique, notamment le Sénégal, la Namibie et le Zimbabwe.

La déclaration d’une urgence de santé publique de portée internationale permettrait une réponse équitable fondée sur les principes et l’éthique de la santé publique : prise en charge et soutien des personnes les plus touchées ; prévention à grande échelle ; et surveillance des conséquences.

Cela permettrait une collaboration internationale, mobiliserait des financements et garantirait une coordination centrale ainsi que le soutien de l’OMS.

Il est temps que les pays déclenchent le processus prévu par le Règlement sanitaire international et qu’un comité d’experts évalue les risques auxquels nous sommes confrontés et formule des recommandations pour y faire face. Il est temps que l’OMS déclare une urgence de santé publique de portée internationale et que nous fassions face ensemble à cette menace en tant que communauté internationale, avant qu’il ne soit trop tard.
