stories.body:
Affordability and small businesses’ economic woes feature heavily in the House race for Wisconsin’s third district

US midterms 2026 live – latest updates

Track live results from all 50 states

After 18 years in business, Erin Klaus is closing her storefront, a handmade artisan market in downtown Eau Claire, Wisconsin , at the end of the year.

She opened Tangled Up in Hue amid a recession, during a time when downtown was “kind of a ghost town”, weathering construction and the pandemic. But the current economic crisis proved too much. She’s seen a downward trend in sales for two years, and was dipping into her own pocket from her other job, as the executive director of business non-profit Downtown Eau Claire Inc, to pay staff.

“This is the first time it’s out of my control to save my business,” she said. “It just feels so desperate right now for a lot of our small business owners … From the tariff wars to inflation to cost of living to healthcare , I mean, honestly, there’s no money left in the bucket at the end of the day for regular folks and, unfortunately, that means our regular folks who run businesses, too, are just not able to kind of hang on any longer.”

These economic woes feature heavily in the toss-up race for the US House of Representatives in western Wisconsin’s third district, where Eau Claire is located. Republican incumbent Derrick Van Orden has stuck closely to Donald Trump and defended the administration’s record, while Democratic challenger Rebecca Cooke is making a third run at the seat by tapping into, and commiserating with, economic despair among working people, farmers and business owners.

Communities like Eau Claire are losing small businesses as people are getting pinched financially and don’t have the extra funds to spend, even if they wanted to, Klaus said. The culture of consumerism changed during the pandemic as well, with people wanting quick, online options. Tariffs on, in her case, T-shirts, forced her to eat the added cost. Healthcare subsidies on the Affordable Care Act marketplace weren’t extended. A paid parking program downtown felt like the final straw. Klaus knows she’s not alone among small business owners.

The messages coming from the Trump administration seem to insist that these economic conditions aren’t happening, or aren’t affecting people like her, to the degree they are, Klaus said. It feels “almost like we’re getting mocked for the hardships that we’re enduring”.

Other small business owners in the district say they’re struggling, too. Amy Burke Lepper, the owner of One Of A Kind Interior Design in Chippewa Falls, has worked with a cabinet maker in Canada for more than two decades, and now those cabinets have added tariffs. A couple of her clients have put off building homes because of costs right now, she said. Her retail shop, Lagom, has been “remarkably slow”. She has no health insurance for the first time in her life because the cost rose from over $1,000 per month for her and her husband to nearly $3,000.

She doesn’t plan to close her business but she decided to speak out about the struggles she’s facing so that people understand how federal policies are affecting small businesses like hers.

“I’m one person, and I know this is affecting everybody else and waking people up to the fact that, you don’t understand that’s why your prices are higher. It’s because of these things. It’s not a magic thing,” Burke Lepper said.

The third district House race

As weeks and months of campaigning have given way to the final days and hours before Tuesday’s US midterm elections, rising prices and affordability have created competitive races in unexpected places. Democrats and independents have found a lane in rural areas stretched thin by gas costs, fertilizer increases, tariffs and healthcare cuts, though the third district was always expected to be competitive.

Before Van Orden’s win in 2022, Democrat Ron Kind had represented the district for more than 20 years. The district, made up of mostly rural and suburban areas, backed Barack Obama twice, then Trump three times, but also sometimes for Democrats elsewhere on the ballot. Tens of millions of dollars in outside spending has poured into the race from both sides.

Trump administration officials have traveled multiple times to the third district in Wisconsin to defend their records. Trump has told his supporters to pretend he is on the ballot this year. Van Orden has defended the Iran war, calling it necessary, though acknowledging it is making it “exponentially harder for Republicans to hold the House and the Senate”.

Mike Johnson, the Republican House speaker, rallied with Van Orden this week, saying he is “one of our fighters”. Van Orden, responding to a reporter, said he hasn’t shied away from his support of Trump. He has been an ardent Trump supporter, including attending the January 6 rally at the US Capitol in 2021.

“At some point, we have to look at accomplishments and put aside the emotional sway,” Van Orden told WISN 12 News . “Donald Trump won this district three times in a row, with increasing margins every single time. The things that he’s been able to accomplish with a Republican-controlled congress is absolutely amazing.”

Van Orden, a retired Navy Seal, refers to his opponent, Cooke, as “The Crooked One”, claiming she isn’t who she says she is. He has posted AI-generated videos of her. When she rallied recently with independent senator Bernie Sanders, who has endorsed her, he called them “cocktail communists”.

His outbursts – both in person and online – throughout his time in the public eye have drawn attention. He threatened a teenage library worker over a pride month display in 2021, screamed at Senate pages at the US Capitol in 2023, and shouted “lies” at Joe Biden during the 2024 state of the union.

Van Orden didn’t respond to requests for an interview or comment.

Translating economic pain into votes

Cooke has emphasized the ways she can relate to the economic despair the voters in the district feel. She grew up on a dairy farm, she said, and her family had to sell their cows because of low milk prices and competition with larger dairies. She ran a small business in Eau Claire. She still works as a waitress. (She also has worked as a political consultant, which Van Orden has used to attack her working-class credentials.) She has been aligned with the centrist Blue Dog Democrats, but got a Sanders endorsement and campaigned on economic populist ideas.

The first thing Democrats should do is expand the Affordable Care Act tax credit premiums that were allowed to expire, for three more years to “stop the hemorrhaging”, Cooke said. She also wants to pass a public option for healthcare and expand Medicare to cover vision, dental and hearing.

The Iran war has “just got to end”, she said, which will help bring down prices. The federal government needs to enforce antitrust laws and take on “corporate conglomerates” that dominate certain industries and break them up, she said. And companies that use AI to surveil customers and set different prices based on this data need to be stopped, she said.

At the restaurant where she works, fewer people are going out to eat because they don’t have spending money, she said. She had to drop her own insurance after the Covid-era subsidies expired. (Van Orden was one of few Republicans to vote to extend them.)

“It just sort of feels like nobody really cares,” Cooke said. “And I think I can talk about those things because I get it. I am in the trenches with everybody else.”

Cooke said she has done the work throughout the district to make her case to voters, and she’ll keep showing up in person for them if she’s elected. She’s gone to small town dairy breakfasts, lutefisk lunches, county fairs, knocked doors. She lost by seven points in 2022, then less than three points in 2024.

“Even if it’s a big blue wave, it will be a ripple here,” she said.

Whatever happens in the election, however, will be too late for Klaus. Tangled Up in Hue will stay open until the end of the year to sell down the products in the store and let the many dozens of artists who sell there earn some money during the holiday season. She’ll keep other aspects of the business open, including an art market on Saturdays, a wholesale element and apparel printing.

Klaus has been a maker since she was a little kid, she said. She’ll find other, new ways to keep that alive. She’s a Democrat, and says she’ll be voting for Cooke for Congress. She hopes more people in the district connect the dots on how their choices for federal offices are hurting the economy now. But, she added, flipping the seat doesn’t immediately resolve all the economic pain.

“This is just a long journey ahead and it’s not going to be a quick fix,” Klaus said. “We need to be able to at least get the people in power that are listening to us and ready to do the hard work that comes next. But it’s certainly not going to be over after 3 November.”

Chinese investors placing high value on AI despite unpopularity of Sanxingdui: Future Past

China’s first fully AI-generated movie has flopped, earning just 1.7m yuan (£191,000) at the box office despite costing “tens of millions” to make, according to its producer.

But is it any good? The Guardian watched Sanxingdui: Future Past in a virtually empty cinema in Beijing, and found it no worse than plenty of human-centred mindless action flicks.

OK, well maybe a bit worse.

Sanxingdui tells a confusing tale of a future society in which every decision has been outsourced to algorithms and AI , leading to a global catastrophe. The only way to avert the impending doom is to unlock the hidden code that is hidden in the Sanxingdui, bronze sculptures linked to the ancient kingdom of Shu. Cue astronauts racing through ancient Egypt and archeologists diving through space-time vortices.

Use of the production company’s in-house AI scriptwriting tool, called Bowen, was evident in lines such as, “That is the superbrain superintelligence that costs $10m dollars a month to subscribe to”, and, “Avoid that thing!” when a plane was about to crash in an incident foretold by the evil algorithm. But the sole other audience member and I agreed that it exceeded our very low expectations.

All of the film’s visuals and some of its sound effects were created using AI, while it was edited by humans.

Many of the characters were uncanny – uncannily life-like for the most part, and uncanny valley for the remainder. The Chinese characters seemed much more realistic than the white people. All of them struggled with running (which they do a lot). They uniformly fell into that steady, smooth gait of video-game characters. One of the main characters, an astronaut called Wu Xingyan, looks creepily like Tilly Norwood , the controversial “AI actor” who is “starring” in an upcoming Hollywood feature film called Misaligned.

But despite Sanxindui’s unpopularity, people who work in the film industry believe that it’s just the beginning of AI cinema in China.

Sanxingdui flopped because “the movie isn’t entertaining”, said Yu Yaqin, an independent film critic in Beijing. At least in the short term, “AI films will continue to be produced in China because investors place a high value on AI,” she said.

One person who works in screenplay development in Beijing said that the majority of projects she has been approached by in the past few months have been for AI films. “Chinese investors believe this is the future,” she said, not least because AI films have the potential to be much cheaper than traditional productions.

“What used to take 100 people to do, now can be done by five people, and the rest won’t have any jobs,” she said.

One state media commentary said that although Sanxingdui was “riddled with flaws and imperfections,” it may “yet go down in cinematic history as the starting point of what came next”.

Chinese audiences are no stranger to AI-generated content. Tens of thousands of AI-generated microdramas, one- to three-minute-long dramas that are designed to be watched on mobile phones, are uploaded to streaming platforms each month. The industry, which didn’t exist a few years ago, is now worth an estimated $3bn. That is still much smaller than the traditional film industry, but a sign of the direction of travel.

Sanxingdui’s poor performance may also be because people don’t want to pay 50 yuan (£5.60) for a cinema ticket when they can watch similar content on their phone for free.

“AI-generated microdramas are selling a way to kill time, while films in cinemas are selling an experience worth spending time on,” wrote one film blogger.

“Perhaps audiences are still more willing to spend money on films that offer a more unique experience,” said Yu, hopefully.

stories.body:
Beijing launches diplomatic salvo to woo Gulf leaders and bolster its influence in the region

China has held a flurry of meetings with Gulf leaders in a sign that Beijing is stepping up its diplomatic efforts in the Middle East.

The diplomatic salvo comes before a highly anticipated meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping when the US president is expected to attend the Apec conference in Shenzhen, China, on 18 and 19 November.

Xi held talks with Haitham bin Tariq , Oman’s sultan, in a historic state visit to Beijing on Monday.

President Xi’s foreign minister, Wang Yi, met Saudi Arabia’s national security adviser, Musaad bin Mohammed Al Aiban, and the deputy secretary of Iran’s national security council, Ali Bagheri Kani.

Haitham’s trip to Beijing is the first time that an Omani head of state has visited China since the two countries established diplomatic relations nearly 50 years ago. According to a Chinese readout of the meeting, Xi warned that the Middle East should not become an arena for “great power rivalry and geopolitical conflicts”.

He said: “China has always been actively committed to stopping conflict and promoting peace, and hopes to contribute wisdom and solutions to resolving the regional security dilemma.”

Wang said after his separate talks that China was willing to “play a constructive role in helping the region emerge from the shadow of the pandemic and achieve lasting peace and stability”. In his meeting with Bagheri Kani, Wang said China supported Iran “in safeguarding its sovereignty and security”. According to China, the Iranian official said his country looked forward to China “playing a more important role in international and regional peace”.

When the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February, China was credited with pushing Tehran toward ceasefire talks in Pakistan , bolstering its status as a regional mediator.

Beijing’s influence in the Middle East is “no longer what it used to be”, said Shen Dingli, a Shanghai-based scholar of international relations. But he added: “Given China’s increased investment and trade in the region … its influence cannot be ignored.”

As the war has dragged on, China’s diplomatic efforts have been muted. Its biggest economic leverage over Iran is the fact that it buys about 90% of the Middle Eastern country’s crude oil exports. Between April and June, it slashed its crude imports by 30%, with the total in June plunging to the lowest level in a decade. That saved the global economy from a major spike in inflation. According to some estimates, China’s cut in oil imports shaved $30 or more off barrel prices of Brent crude, a global benchmark.

Beijing has otherwise done little to broker peace in the Middle East. That is partly because it does not see the conflict as being its responsibility to resolve. In March, Wang said the war “should never have happened” and that the US and Israel would find “no popular support” for the strikes.

China is also a beneficiary from the damage that the fighting has done to the US’s global reputation.

According to findings published in July by the Pew Research Center, a Washington-based thinktank, China is now viewed more favourably than the US in a majority of 36 countries surveyed.

The pain caused by the long-term disruption to the strait of Hormuz, the waterway through which much of the world’s oil and gas flows, also poses a risk to China’s economy. Shortages of energy cause inflation, which risks reducing global demand for Chinese goods.

Tehran and Washington are locked in intensive talks to reach an agreement, which could include reopening the strait. Trump has repeatedly threatened to renew military action against Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US, a move which would cause alarm in Beijing.

Trump’s desperation to reach a deal in the Middle East may also provide an opportunity for China to present itself as a regional peacemaker, bolstering Xi’s status before their meeting. Beijing brokered a detente between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023 but since then its diplomatic impact in the region has been limited.

Shen said China’s desire to improve diplomatic relations with Middle Eastern countries as well as the US were “mutually reinforcing” trends.

China’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning, said on Monday that China would send special envoy Zhai Jun to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November.

stories.title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
stories.summary: The food deal, ahead of a UK-EU summit later this month, is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 3 November 2026

The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month.

The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders.

The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market.

As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.

Speaking during the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, the prime minister said a UK-EU deal could add up to 0.4% extra on GDP.

The deal could have the following impact:

Exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes would be able to resume

It should remove the need for £200 Export Health Certificates, which confirm the product meets the health requirements of the country it is heading to

It should also end the need for £25 Phytosanitary certificates, which show that plants or plant products are free from pests and diseases

Inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU could be removed

It will bring back passports for British pets being taken into the EU

In return, the UK is expected to commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards - a process called "dynamic alignment".

Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July.

Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his.

At Chogm on Tuesday, Burnham said: "I think people in Britain would expect me to take that with both hands, given where we've been in recent times, and that's what I'm doing."

Pressed on whether it would be acceptable for the UK to have its rules on food trade made by the EU, he said: "We're not in the EU, therefore we do have to work with them in a different way.

"But if that can get growth, if that can help our farmers, if that can remove red tape from British businesses, I think most people would expect me to go to that summit and negotiate the best deal that I can.

"And that's what I've been doing in recent weeks, leaning in, being positive, having a really constructive relationship with our European partners and hopefully we can land a good deal for Britain in terms of growth but also I hope more collaboration on controlling immigration."

Jon Walsh of Bio&Me said his firm had stopped exporting yoghurt due to vets' fees

Jon Walsh, the chief executive and co-founder of Bio&Me, which makes granolas, mueslis and yoghurts, told BBC 5 Live the draft deal sounded like "really good news".

"We're just a small company but when we were trying to export our yoghurts before, every time we'd send a pallet we had to pay a vet to inspect it and that was £140, and that meant that you'd lose money... so we had to stop."

The company also had problems exporting granola and overnight oats, with some shipments being returned.

"It was so frustrating because it was the same person filling out the same form and yet half would make it through and half wouldn't," Walsh said.

"You just kind of give up because you're losing money."

In an interview with ITV, Burnham said "public opinion has changed nationally" since the 2016 Brexit vote, but added he would "not run ahead of public opinion" on the issue.

"The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit," he added.

Burnham also said he had not proposed the return of freedom of movement between the UK and EU.

Asked by the BBC about the UK's relationship with the EU, Tory Leader Kemi Badenoch said that while we should "work closely", "dynamic alignment" with the EU would be a red line and "actually take us backwards".

Liberal Democrat Europe spokesperson Al Pinkerton said the draft deal was a "patch, not a fix".

"The real solution is to rejoin the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU," he added.

Reform UK's business spokesman Richard Tice said: "One of the key benefits of Brexit was that Britain no longer had to adhere to ridiculous EU rules.

"Returning to any form of alignment with Europe would crush Britain's competitiveness and force us to surrender sovereignty over trade policy, putting trade deals worth hundreds of billions of pounds at risk."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen with Prime Minister Andy Burnham

While UK rules remain mostly aligned with EU ones, there are some areas where England has diverged from the EU rule book, for example on "precision breeding" of plants, previously known as gene editing. In recent weeks, agreement has been struck on transition arrangements while the EU's new regulations come in to force.

The government has already announced a European Partnerships Bill which will provide a legal mechanism for the application of new EU rules and regulations. This will also allow for the necessary alignments for the linking of the UK emissions trading scheme with the EU's, and save the need for UK exporters to pay the EU's new carbon border tax.

The draft agreements will be discussed at a meeting of EU ambassadors called Coreper on Wednesday, with some key details on the planned numbers in a Youth Experience Scheme to be finalised at a political level in the coming days. A discount on full foreign student fees for EU students is likely to be pushed to next year alongside a plan to reconnect electricity markets.

The BBC understands the draft agreements will also include some references to UK involvement in defence co-operation schemes, access to law enforcement databases and some reassurances over the EU's "Made in Europe" plans .

A food deal will have particular significance for Northern Ireland, radically reducing the impact of the post-Brexit Irish Sea border.

Northern Ireland's Brexit deal kept it inside the EU's single market for goods. That means food products from elsewhere in the UK require paperwork and some physical checks when arriving at NI's ports. A deal will ultimately end those requirements.

While the food trade plans have been backed by supermarkets and farmers representatives, some pro-Brexit campaigners have criticised the reapplication of EU rules. The post-Brexit trade deal signed by Boris Johnson's government prioritised regulatory freedoms for the UK over avoiding new regulatory red tape, checks and delays.

But William Bain, the British Chamber of Commerce's (BCC) head of trade policy, told the BBC's Today programme that business overall thought it was a "price is worth paying" to follow common rules, as companies would benefit from "lower costs, reduced delays [and] increased market access".

At the moment, he said, the requirement for Export Health Certificates can add thousands of pounds of costs to each truck carrying goods, in addition "to the delays that people find at the ports or at the borders".

"So we get lower exports because of the delays and the massive increases in costs that have come into the supply chain."

The BCC has released a new analysis of its members' views suggesting options for a closer relationship.

The business lobby group says the current trade relationship is "failing to deliver", leaving firms "struggling with a thicket of Brexit red tape" nearly six years after the UK's exit from the bloc.

Watch: King says slave trade a 'shameful chapter' that 'fills my heart with horror'

Published 3 November 2026

King Charles has described the transatlantic slave trade as a "shameful chapter of history" that filled him with "profound sorrow" as he opened a summit of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.

He said the trade in enslaved persons "still casts a shadow" over the association of nations.

There have been calls from some for the UK to make a formal apology for its historic role in the slave trade ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, but there was not one in the King's address.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, also at the summit, has said that he is open to Britain issuing a formal apology but has ruled out financial reparations.

While there was no direct apology, the King did offer some contrition - and there was also an acknowledgement that he had personally learnt more about the legacy of the slave trade.

He said: "The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth.

"As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."

He told the summit: "The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future."

King Charles continued: "History is not ours to choose or to change. It is bequeathed to us in complex synthesis by forebears we can never know.

"Our inheritance includes both their achievements and their failures – the good they did as well as the wrongs."

The King's address also referenced the "brutal conflicts" the world is facing, the "catastrophic reality" of climate and rapid technological development.

The Chogm meeting gathers leaders from 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth, a voluntary grouping made up primarily of former territories of the British Empire.

The biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.

Speaking on Tuesday, Burnham said his government was bringing a new approach, aiming to "revitalise the Commonwealth", despite turning down demands for reparations.

"I've been very clear that we do not support reparations," he said.

"But it's not the case that we don't support countries in the Commonwealth around development, and helping them with debt issues that they've got, green finance.

"That's what we've done under all governments and in my view we should continue to do as part of being a Commonwealth."

The King and Queen are on a tour of the Caribbean which has reignited difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.

On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".

In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion, where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.

stories.summary: The original version fell in July in a row over spending on additional learning needs education.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Plaid and Labour previously failed to agree on spending on support for children with additional learning needs

Published 3 November 2026

The Senedd has passed the Welsh government's mini-budget, nearly four months after the original version was defeated, following a deal between Plaid Cymru ministers and Labour.

Under the agreement, announced in October , an extra £60m will be spent on supporting children with additional learning needs (ALN).

Labour, now in opposition after heavy election losses , had rejected a £40m package spread over three years in July, with leader Ken Skates demanding £100m this financial year instead.

By voting for the extra spending plans on Tuesday evening Labour gave the minority Plaid government the numbers it needed.

Plaid Cymru's original mini-budget also included £100m for the NHS to bring down waiting times, £55m for childcare and £40m for school repairs, spending that can now go ahead.

Former Welsh Labour leader Mark Drakeford previously said his party had made mistakes in its summer negotiations with Plaid, and suggested there was a case for accepting the money previously offered by the government.

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth agreed his government had learned lessons from its failure to reach a deal in July.

Finance Minister Elin Jones began the debate "by recognising the constructive discussions that have taken place in recent weeks with the Labour group".

On ALN, she said: "While there have been differing views on how best to respond there has been a broad recognition that these pressures are real and require action. That shared understanding has enabled agreement to be reached."

Reform's finance spokesperson, Cai Parry Jones, criticised Labour for "somehow backing this budget" despite the NAHT teaching union being in dispute with the government.

"Ken, who is really pulling the strings in Welsh Labour?" he said, suggesting Mark Drakeford's views on the budget may have been influential behind the scenes.

He called for foreign spending to be cut back.

Huw Thomas, Labour's finance spokesperson, said the process of agreeing a supplementary budget had been more difficult than it should have been.

But he said Plaid had seemed to have learned "lessons", and Labour had secured 50% more on ALN than Plaid Cymru had put on the table in the summer.

Calling for the money to be made available as soon as possible, he said: "Schools cannot afford lengthy delays and bureaucratic obstacles."

Welsh Conservative Peter Fox said: "We were told a Plaid Cymru government would be different,", confirming his party would vote against the budget.

"The budget just seems to be business as usual wrapped in different colours."

The budget motion was passed in the Senedd with 54 votes in support and 39 against.

The Athenian led the people, he didn’t follow them, writes Prof Costas Milas

Your editorial ( The Guardian view on a changing Brexit debate: Kemi Badenoch is trapped in denial, 29 October ) notes that when it comes to Brexit, Andy Burnham appears to be following the voters. This, in my humble opinion, is a problem. Thucydides noted about Pericles, the Athenian statesman, that “it was he who led them [the people], rather than they who led him”.

It was arguably the constant and thoughtful guidance of Pericles to his fellow Athenian citizens that made Athens the dominant political and economic power, respected by its friends and enemies alike. Burnham needs to take the lead and show his cards on what type of relationship he wants to pursue with our European partners. To do so, he could start by asking the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) to produce an independent and authoritative analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of the different types of closer relationship with the EU.

The analysis should consider the potential impact of measures of UK economic policy uncertainty , which spiked during the Brexit referendum and remained notably elevated afterwards. The analysis should also model the very structural change currently taking place in the UK economy. Had there been no structural change (either abrupt or slow-moving), there wouldn’t have been any reason for voting in favour of Brexit in the first place.

The OBR has the knowledge and expertise to model the economic impact of the UK’s return to the EU. Burnham could then use the analysis to make his case to voters and lead the way, as Pericles would have done. Prof Costas Milas University of Liverpool

For example, Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor’s race on a ticket of wanting an immediate moratorium on data centre buildouts. Given AI’s role in powering the US economy, speculation over whether a new Democrat Congress would slow AI capital expenditure plans briefly hit markets. The chip exporter-heavy stock markets of Korea and Taiwan were briefly down 3-4% overnight on news of the blue wave, but have since recouped all those losses. For bond investors, the significance of the midterms is ultimately about what they mean for US borrowing. The result makes further significant fiscal expansion harder to deliver through Congress, potentially easing some of the pressure around government borrowing and Treasury issuance. That could be supportive for US Treasuries, but it won’t determine the direction of yields on its own. Growth, inflation and the Federal Reserve remain crucial. If the economy slows and inflation continues to ease, there is a stronger case for Treasury yields to move lower. European shares rise as Democratic sweep lifts clean energy and bank stocks

Over here, stock markets have risen this morning, with banks and clean energy stocks leading the gains. The FTSE 100 index in London is 24 points, or 0.2% ahead.

The pan-European SToxx 600 index gained 0.6%, with Germany’s Dax almost 0.6% ahead and France’s CAC up 0.4%, and Italy’s FTSE MiB index jumping almost 1.4%.

Bank stocks leapt 2.8% and clean energy stocks, which have borne the brunt of Donald Trump ’s policies, were also among the top risers. Denmark’s Vestas Wind Systems jumped about 5% and Ørsted surged 7.4% while the German wind turbine company Nordex leapt 6.5%.

European defence stocks fell, while European tech stocks recovered to trade 0.5% higher.

Democrats have taken control of both the Senate and House of Representatives and scored victories in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations, as voters rejected Trump’s agenda.

This ushers in an era of divided government in Washington, following two years in which the Republican-controlled Congress rarely reined in Trump.

Investors are assessing the prospect of tougher US regulation on the booming AI sector (where fears over ballooning debt levels to fund the infrastructure buildout have already led to selloffs in recent months), higher taxes and oversight of cryptocurrencies.

Shares of big technology companies Amazon , Google owner Alphabet , Microsoft and Meta Platforms , the parent company behind Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram, declined on the Tradegate platform in Europe, according to Reuters. Elon Musk ’s Tesla and SpaceX both fell between 4.5% and 5%.

Kathleen Brooks , research director at the trading platform XTB, says:

double quotation mark Overall, these results have had a mild impact on markets so far. Investors will move on from trading the uncertainty of the election results to trading the reality of what they mean for policy. This is bad news for Tesla and SpaceX on Wednesday, but the semiconductor names, the backbone of the AI trade, could brush off concerns about AI regulation ‌and continue to move higher after Tuesday’s stunning rally for the sector.

However, Aidan Yao , senior investment strategist for Asia at the Amundi Investment Institute, told Reuters:

double quotation mark The significance of these midterm elections is more like a referendum on AI than a referendum on Trump. If the AI theme is subject to some restrictions, then the US economy, US inflation and US monetary policy all become very, very uncertain.

The price of gold , seen as a safe haven in times of uncertainty, jumped 3% to $4,046 an ounce (for spot gold).

Sterling hits seven-week high against dollar

Sterling has hit a seven-week high against the dollar, which weakened across the board following the mid-term election results.

The pound climbed 0.6% to $1.3495 earlier and is now up 0.5% at $1.3483. It also firmed slightly against the euro, to 83.43 pence.

Sterling is also underpinned by expectations of interest rate hikes from the Bank of England, which is expected to raise borrowing costs from 3.75% to 4% at its meeting tomorrow. Higher rates usually boost a currency because they lead to be better returns for investors.

Markets are expecting three more quarter-point rate hikes in the coming 12 months.

This means more than 2.3m UK households face a sharp rise in mortgage payments as they come off fixed-rate deals next year.

Cryptocurrencies recover from earlier losses

Cryptocurrencies initially fell but then recovered, after the Democrats won control of both houses of ⁠the US Congress in the ⁠midterm elections – seen as a potential ​blow to an industry that has sought faster deregulation for digital assets.

While Donald Trump has been championing reduced regulation, some Democrats have also backed a light-touch ⁠approach.

The crypto sector spent more than $300m backing crypto-friendly Democrat and Republican politicians during the current and previous election cycles, according to Reuters.

Bitcoin, the world’s best-known cryptocurrency, briefly touched a six-week low before recovering to trade 0.8% higher on the ⁠day at $78,460. This came after a reversal in the stock market, where US index futures were up 0.3%, having fallen as much ​as 2% at one point overnight. Ether gained 1.4% to trade ‌at $2,323.

Bitcoin has fallen around 41% ‌since reaching record highs above $122,000 in October 2025, taking the value of the broader crypto market to about $2.6 trillion, according to CoinMarketCap.

Arun Pillai-Essex , principal geopolitical analyst at the risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, has looked at the impact on US trade policy .

He argues the US midterms point to a significant shift in the political landscape, with implications extending well beyond Washington. This is particularly the case for key trading partners and emerging markets in Asia, where US trade and technology policy has an outsized impact on investment and economic growth.

double quotation mark With affordability dominating the midterm debate, we expect growing bipartisan pressure for tariff relief, particularly from lawmakers representing agricultural states and areas with strong trade ties to Canada. We’ve already seen selective exemptions on Canadian imports ahead of the elections. We expect Congress to become more assertive on trade policy , challenging tariffs through disapproval resolutions and greater oversight. While presidential veto powers limit their direct impact, growing bipartisan opposition could raise the political costs of further escalation. However, we don’t expect a fundamental shift in the White House approach. Tariffs remain an important bargaining tool, and further duties targeting manufacturing overcapacity across 16 major economies remain likely, adding another layer of restrictions following the forced labour tariffs imposed earlier this year. The proposed overcapacity tariffs have a significant focus on Southeast Asia and the wider APAC region, adding to the trade pressures already facing regional exporters. A divided Washington is unlikely to offer much relief, with protectionist headwinds continuing to complicate trade and investment decisions across the region. Overall, we expect the broader tariff framework to remain largely intact, but with greater scope for selective exemptions and negotiated concessions, while the White House keeps the threat of further escalation on the table.

Turning to AI policy , he says:

double quotation mark Datacentre opposition cuts across party lines, driven by concerns over electricity, water and other local impacts. We’re already seeing this translate into state-level action, with New York and Texas moving to restrict new developments and growing scrutiny over who ultimately foots the bill. In a divided Washington, these concerns are likely to gain further political traction, particularly as both parties look to capitalise on public unease around AI. The debate over datacentres is increasingly feeding into a wider debate about the pace of AI adoption and its economic and social costs. However, we don’t expect the growing political backlash to significantly slow AI investment. Instead, developers are likely to face greater pressure to shoulder infrastructure costs, alongside tighter conditions on new projects. But the underlying tension isn’t going away. Washington wants to accelerate AI investment to maintain its technological lead, while state and local governments face growing pressure to protect households from high costs. At the federal level, a divided government will sharpen tensions with Congress and the White House over US tech policy. Two areas to watch closely are advanced semiconductor export controls and restrictions on outbound US investment into sensitive technologies. The central tension over semiconductor exports is between Congress pushing for tighter, legally binding restrictions and a White House seeking to preserve flexibility to negotiate, selectively ease controls and protect US commercial interests.

And Chris Turner , global head of markets at ING, says:

double quotation mark Investors will be parsing what this all means. For example, Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor’s race on a ticket of wanting an immediate moratorium on data centre buildouts. Given AI’s role in powering the US economy, speculation over whether a new Democrat Congress would slow AI capital expenditure plans briefly hit markets. The chip exporter-heavy stock markets of Korea and Taiwan were briefly down 3-4% overnight on news of the blue wave, but have since recouped all those losses. That the initial market moves are being reversed probably owes to the fact that the Democrats do not take office until January. Also, one wild-card risk removed from the dollar’s downside has been president Trump accepting these results. However, overnight price action could provide a preview for markets in 2027. We had felt that a Democrat Congress would be a mild dollar negative – both in terms of what it would mean for the AI story and the prospect of a prolonged US government shutdown potentially from next summer. Before then, however, investors are faced with a strong US economy and a Fed ready to tighten further. US labour market data has come in on the strong side so far this week. Fresh insights will be seen today in the release of the monthly ADP figure and the employment component in the October ISM services.

US Treasuries rally on prospect of reduced government spending

US government bonds have rallied, pushing yields down, as investors were relieved that Democrats’ capture of Congress could limit Donald Trump ’s spending plans.

The yield, or interest rate, on the benchmark 10-year US treasury bond fell 4.7 basis points to 4.918%, while the two-year bond yield dropped 3.7bps to 4.597%. Yields fall when bond prices rise.

Analysts said tougher regulation of the AI sector could lead to slower economic growth, but also reduce the need for interest rate hikes.

The dollar has weakened as a result, and is currently trading 0.5% lower against a basket of six other major currencies.

Oliver Faizallah , head of fixed income research at the US investment bank Raymond James, says:

double quotation mark For bond investors, the significance of the midterms is ultimately about what they mean for US borrowing. The result makes further significant fiscal expansion harder to deliver through Congress, potentially easing some of the pressure around government borrowing and Treasury issuance. That could be supportive for US Treasuries, but it won’t determine the direction of yields on its own. Growth, inflation and the Federal Reserve remain crucial. If the economy slows and inflation continues to ease, there is a stronger case for Treasury yields to move lower.

And Prashant Newnaha , senior rates strategist at TD Securities in Singapore, says:

double quotation mark Bonds are coming out ​as the clear winner as markets put the AI trade on the ​chopping block and embrace the higher possibility that further tax ​cuts are put on ice and government spending slows.

European shares rise as Democratic sweep lifts clean energy and bank stocks

Over here, stock markets have risen this morning, with banks and clean energy stocks leading the gains. The FTSE 100 index in London is 24 points, or 0.2% ahead.

The pan-European SToxx 600 index gained 0.6%, with Germany’s Dax almost 0.6% ahead and France’s CAC up 0.4%, and Italy’s FTSE MiB index jumping almost 1.4%.

Bank stocks leapt 2.8% and clean energy stocks, which have borne the brunt of Donald Trump ’s policies, were also among the top risers. Denmark’s Vestas Wind Systems jumped about 5% and Ørsted surged 7.4% while the German wind turbine company Nordex leapt 6.5%.

European defence stocks fell, while European tech stocks recovered to trade 0.5% higher.

Democrats have taken control of both the Senate and House of Representatives and scored victories in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations, as voters rejected Trump’s agenda.

This ushers in an era of divided government in Washington, following two years in which the Republican-controlled Congress rarely reined in Trump.

Investors are assessing the prospect of tougher US regulation on the booming AI sector (where fears over ballooning debt levels to fund the infrastructure buildout have already led to selloffs in recent months), higher taxes and oversight of cryptocurrencies.

Shares of big technology companies Amazon , Google owner Alphabet , Microsoft and Meta Platforms , the parent company behind Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram, declined on the Tradegate platform in Europe, according to Reuters. Elon Musk ’s Tesla and SpaceX both fell between 4.5% and 5%.

Kathleen Brooks , research director at the trading platform XTB, says:

double quotation mark Overall, these results have had a mild impact on markets so far. Investors will move on from trading the uncertainty of the election results to trading the reality of what they mean for policy. This is bad news for Tesla and SpaceX on Wednesday, but the semiconductor names, the backbone of the AI trade, could brush off concerns about AI regulation ‌and continue to move higher after Tuesday’s stunning rally for the sector.

However, Aidan Yao , senior investment strategist for Asia at the Amundi Investment Institute, told Reuters:

double quotation mark The significance of these midterm elections is more like a referendum on AI than a referendum on Trump. If the AI theme is subject to some restrictions, then the US economy, US inflation and US monetary policy all become very, very uncertain.

The price of gold , seen as a safe haven in times of uncertainty, jumped 3% to $4,046 an ounce (for spot gold).

US stock futures turn positive

US stock futures have turned positive ahead of the Wall Street open later, as investors continue to assess the implications of the blue wave across the US, with the Democrats winning control of Congress.

Dow Jones futures are up 0.4%, while S&P 500 and futures for the tech-heavy Nasdaq have both edged about 0.15% higher.

Earlier, Nasdaq futures fell 2.4% while S&P 500 futures dropped 1.4%.

Democrats won governorship races in Texas and Georgia, key states for AI datacentres. Many Americans worry about their massive energy use and impact on water consumption and pollution.

Democrats' Texas win spells trouble for datacentres, analysts say

The Texas win for the Democrats spells trouble for datacentres , analysts say.

According to Chris Beauchamp , chief market analyst at IG in London:

double quotation mark Greg Abbott ’s loss of the Texas governorship means that the construction of more data centres is now open to question. We saw this overnight with weakness in the AI stocks like CoreWeave and Nebius , and while there has been some recovery the questions about how this plays out will continue to dog a sector already grappling with spending worries. Now legislation concerns are on the list too.

Tapas Strickland , chief market strategist at the investing platform Moomoo ANZ in Sydney, told Reuters earlier:

double quotation mark I think the fear is that the pace of the AI infrastructure rollout could slow, potentially quite markedly in Texas, as they start to digest exactly what mandate they might have in terms of AI. Going into this, we were talking about the importance of the Texas and Georgia governor races. Those two states effectively make up about a third of all AI datacentre spend and projects. If both of those go Democrat at the governor level [they did], the potential for it to slow is very much there, and that would obviously cascade through to the rest of the AI sector.

Christopher Hodg e, chief US economist at Natixis in New York, says:

double quotation mark Economically, we still don’t think the direct implications are huge. That doesn’t mean that [last night] won’t have big implications. For one thing, Trump doesn’t like bad news and seeing as how he personally selected many of the struggling candidates, he might be looking to change the narrative sooner rather than later. A ‘short and intense’ campaign in Iran has been rumoured ... and that would certainly be a distraction. Presidents typically start making changes after midterms anyway and Trump could be looking for scapegoats. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth comes to mind as a possibility. Bessent is another one to watch...he may be looking for a graceful exit if he views the administration as a sinking ship.

Deborah Cunningham , chief investment officer of global liquidity markets at Federated Hermes, says:

double quotation mark Democrats pulled off a double victory in the US midterm elections that few saw coming at the onset of the year. The blue wave means the federal government is sure to be divided on most issues. That typically creates a blockade against new legislation — an environment which broad financial markets traditionally view favorably as variables decrease. But liquidity investors are different: they primarily look to the US Federal Reserve headquarters further down the National Mall from the Capitol for guidance – and its perspective is unlikely to have changed. The Fed might have wanted to hike rates in October due to stubbornly high inflation, but that policy-setting meeting may have been too close to the election. (Market sentiment has it that Fed officials traditionally have avoided rate moves in those periods to avoid seeming biased to a political party.) That stance, and officials penciling one more increase in 2026 in their September Summary of Economic Projections, could mean a quarter-point hike in December. That would raise the fed funds target range to 4.00-4.25%. That scenario would be music to the ears of cash investors, as the yields of most liquidity products have the potential to rise in concert with Fed hikes. And additional tightening in 2027 is likely. Why? Due to the lag between policy moves and their impact on the broad economy, inflation might not decline for several quarters. Also, the Fed tends to adjust policy in cycles rather than intermittently. But even if rates stay at present levels, industry liquidity offerings should, we believe, remain attractive.

The Democrats have taken control of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections. What does this mean for investors?

Steven Chiavarone , chief investment officer for global equities at Federated Hermes, says:

double quotation mark Prior to the US midterm elections, we felt that only two outcomes could meaningfully change monetary and fiscal policy: a GOP sweep creating wider voting margins or a Democratic blue wave large enough to produce filibuster- and veto-proof majorities. While the Democrats have retaken both chambers of Congress, it appears not to be enough to create the latter scenario. In the coming weeks, the stock market may experience volatility, but we think it should ultimately rise. Historically, the 12 months following midterm elections have been good for US equities. In fact, it has been 88 years since the S&P 500 last posted a negative return in that period, with an average of 14%. Why? One explanation is that the poor result of the president’s party motivates it to champion economic policies that improve its chance of victory in the next presidential election. Another is that a divided government hinders the sort of drastic legislation that can unsettle investors, though this election outcome actually raises the odds of modestly stimulative policy passing. While the present uncertainty and changing of the guard might make investors anxious, no US midterm election has ended the world, and this one will not either. We are looking past the noise, focusing on the real opportunities due to strong economic growth, significant infrastructure buildout and what may be the earnings cycle of our lifetime.

'Blue wave washes over US, futures recover', analysts say

Chris Beauchamp , chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, says:

double quotation mark Overnight markets had pointed towards steep losses for futures, but the picture is looking rosier as markets seem to look towards the future with relish. A divided US government has often been the best outcome for markets, and we are staring that squarely in the face today. Gold and silver are up, while volatility has reversed course too. All eyes are on the White House now, but Trump’s apparent acceptance of the results at least suggests a nasty litigation battle (or worse) is off the cards.

And Axel Rudolph , chief technical analyst at IG, adds:

double quotation mark Midterms rattle Trump, send dollar lower and bullion higher: The heavy Republican defeat is a stark reminder that even a president who dominates the political conversation is not immune to voter discontent. The scale of the losses will inevitably raise questions about Trump’s ability to push through his agenda over the next two years, and markets are already reacting. The dollar is under pressure as investors reassess the political outlook, while gold and silver are benefiting as safe haven plays. A divided government may ultimately prove manageable for markets, but the immediate message is clear: investors are becoming less comfortable with the political risks surrounding the White House.

Introduction: Dollar falls while gold and US Treasury bonds rally as markets react to Democrats’ midterm election victory

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

The dollar has hit a one-month low, US stock futures are down and gold rose after the Democrats won control of Congress, increasing expectations of tougher regulation of the AI sector.

US Treasuries rallied as fears around the fiscal outlook eased and investors sought the safety of bonds with the dollar falling.

Democrats regained control of the Senate and also triumphed in the House of Representatives, routing Republicans nationwide with historic victories that will give them powerful new leverage over Donald Trump for the remainder of his presidency.

You can follow the latest on our midterm election blog here:

The dollar fell 0.6% against a basket of major currencies at one stage, and is now down 0.35%. Its decline was most pronounced against the Japanese yen and the Swiss franc, both seen as safe-haven currencies.

Gold prices ​rose 2.4%, supported by the weaker US dollar. Spot gold climbed to $4,022 an ounce.

US stock futures fell sharply, with tech-heavy Nasdaq futures losing more than 2% before paring those losses to 0.25%. S&P 500 futures are down 0.2%.

In bond markets, the two-year Treasury yield fell 3.5 basis points overnight and is now down 1.6bps at 4.598%, while the 10-year yield is 2bps lower at 4.929%. Yields move in opposite direction to prices.

Jim Reid , head of global macro at Deutsche Bank, explains:

double quotation mark There’s been a rally for US Treasuries as well, given that divided government has generally made it harder for fiscal stimulus to be passed. So that’s eased concerns on the fiscal trajectory a bit. Investors are also pricing in a more dovish path for the Federal Reserve too, with the amount of rate hikes priced by the June 2027 meeting down 3.3bps this morning to 55bps. So that’s pushed the dollar index down.

In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei lost 1.4% while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 1.3% and South Korea’s Kospi gained 0.4%.

Stephen Brown , chief North America economist at Capital Economics, says:

double quotation mark The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation. But the Democrats will now hold Senate seats in many typically red states for the next six years, which increases their chance of being able to enact more sweeping legislative changes if they win the next presidential election. That includes the potential for tax hikes on corporations and high-income individuals as well as regulation that could delay the AI rollout.

stories.title: What are the planned changes to immigration rules?
stories.summary: The home secretary sets out plans to change requirements for permanent settlement in the UK.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood set out the plans in the House of Commons

Published 2 November 2026

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has set out plans to overhaul immigration rules.

Proposals for stricter requirements to qualify for permanent settlement in the UK were first outlined in detail in November 2025, when Mahmood was home secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government.

She has argued that settlement should be "earned", rather than being granted automatically, with those who contribute more to the country able to settle fastest.

Following a consultation , external , Mahmood has now announced her final decision on what changes should be taken forward.

Elements of her original proposals have been revised following a backlash from some Labour MPs, with plans to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait 15 years to qualify for settlement scrapped.

Mahmood scraps settlement plans for migrant care workers Published 1 day ago

Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes Published 1 day ago

What is settlement and indefinite leave to remain?

Indefinite leave to remain (ILR) – also known as settlement – gives someone the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like.

Under the current system, people with ILR can also apply for benefits if they are eligible.

People who have lived in the UK for 12 months after being given ILR can apply for British citizenship, if they also meet other requirements , external .

How will the new rules affect migrants?

Under the government's plans, the standard length of time migrants will have to live in the UK to qualify for permanent settlement will double from five to 10 years.

Under this 10-year pathway, applicants must have earned at least £12,571 for five of the seven years immediately before being granted settlement.

However, there will be a shorter qualifying period of five years for certain groups, including:

People who earned at least £50,271 for three of five years immediately before applying for settlement

Care workers who earned at least £25,000 a year while meeting their visa conditions and arrived in the UK before May 2025

"Skilled" public service workers in health and education, such as doctors, nurses, teachers and social workers

Other health and education public service workers who fall below this skill level, for example nursing auxiliaries and teaching assistants, if they arrived in the UK before May 2025

People from Hong Kong who hold British National (Overseas) status

People earning over £125,141 a year, as well as "highly skilled" migrants such as those on Global Talent or Innovator Founder visas, will qualify after three years.

Migrants who have claimed certain benefits or breached immigration rules will only be able to settle after at least 20 years.

Adults with a criminal record will be refused settlement, with discretion to refuse cases where the offence was committed when the applicant was under 18.

To qualify for settlement, migrants will generally also have to meet other conditions, including:

Speak English to a high standard

Owe no debt to the government, such as unpaid taxes

Earn at least £12,571 a year for at least three years, aligned with the threshold for paying income tax

Some care workers will be able to qualify for settlement after five years

What about refugees?

There will be a different set of rules for refugees – people who have been granted asylum in the UK because they are unable to return to their own country as they fear persecution.

Refugees who arrived in the UK through an official government scheme will qualify for settlement after five years.

However, other refugees will need to wait 10 years and either work or study.

Those who do not work or study will need to wait 20 years.

Refugees who arrived in the UK by small boat or another illegal route will have to wait 20 years if they work or study, and 30 years if they don't.

Will migrants already in the UK be affected?

The changes will apply to migrants who are already in the UK but not those who have already been granted settlement.

What about family members?

A partner who arrives with someone who then applies for ILR will be able to settle at the same time, as long as they meet the relevant requirements.

However, a partner who joins later will need to complete the same qualifying residence period before they are eligible for settlement.

Eligible couples will be able to combine their earnings to meet the minimum income requirement.

The household income threshold will be £25,142 – twice the individual minimum income requirement.

Children under 18 will continue to be able to settle with their parents.

They will be exempt from the income, government debt, English language and Life in the UK test requirements, but will remain subject to the relevant suitability and criminality requirements.

Young adults aged 18 to 24, who remain dependant on their family, will also continue to be able to settle alongside them.

They will be expected to meet all the adult mandatory requirements but not the individual income requirement.

Someone who is aged 25 or over when their family becomes eligible for settlement will be expected to qualify independently.

Eligible partners, parents and children of British citizens will continue to qualify for settlement after five years.

stories.title: Mahmood refuses to put cost on care worker settlement climbdown
stories.summary: The home secretary says the full cost of dropping plans to extend the wait for settlement will be laid out in future.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood revised her settlement reforms after a backlash from some Labour MPs

Published 3 November 2026

The home secretary has declined to specify how much scrapping her plan to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait longer to qualify for permanent settlement will cost.

Shabana Mahmood had originally proposed doubling the wait from five years to 10 for most migrants, with some facing a 15-year wait, which the Home Office suggested could save £10bn.

But under revised plans described by the Tories as a "U-turn", some foreign care workers will continue to wait five years, and others will be able to seek a five-year extension.

While not detailing the cost of the revised plans, Mahmood told the BBC they would still save "billions" because workers in other sectors would have to wait longer.

In March, the Home Office said , external the net lifetime cost of care workers and their adult dependants expected to settle between 2026 and 2030 was estimated at £10bn under existing rules.

Mahmood was proposing to delay settlement for this cohort in response to concerns over record post-Brexit net migration figures under the previous Tory government - dubbed the "Boriswave" by critics.

She had previously argued that not delaying settlement for migrant care workers already in the UK would lead to a "£10bn drain on our public finances".

Following a backlash, Mahmood announced on Monday that care workers who arrived in the UK before May 2025 and earned at least £25,000 a year would continue to qualify after five years, alongside some other groups.

Foreign care workers who do not qualify for the five-year settlement will be able to apply for a new five-year visa, and then seek settlement.

Just over 500,000 people will now be delayed from gaining permanent residency, down from almost 800,000 before Monday's changes. Some 1.9m people will settle in the UK between 2026 and 2030, according to the Home Office.

Indefinite leave to remain (ILR), also known as settlement, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. They can also use it to apply for British citizenship.

No new cost figure yet

Asked about the cost of her revised plans, the home secretary told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the detailed costs would be published when her department puts the changes before Parliament.

In an interview recorded on Monday evening, she said the changes overall represented "savings in the billions" to the Department of Work and Pensions in people not claiming benefits.

"The reason for that is the cohort that was most likely to fall upon the state is that cohort of care workers not doing care work at the moment - if they'd settled at five years, many more of those would have gone on to claim benefits.

"That will now not happen because they will not be settling at five years - those individuals get a second chance to make that contribution that they originally came to make," she told Today.

The Home Office's £10bn figure was based on an estimate by the Migration Advisory Committee of how much an average migrant care worker would cost the UK in benefits and public services throughout their lifetime.

While Mahmood would not give a new savings figure, Home Office minister Anna Turley told BBC Breakfast it would be "at least £1bn over the next couple of years in terms of welfare savings" but "we'll be doing more calculations" on the total.

The Conservatives said the "U-turn" would cost the UK billions of pounds.

Most people who come to the UK do so legally, after being granted a visa before they travel.

A visa gives someone permission to enter or stay in the UK for a specific purpose, such as work, study or joining family members.

There were 727,487 people who came to the UK via visas from July 2025 to June 2026, not including visitors or people transiting through the UK. This was down by 15% on the same period the previous year.

That does not mean all those people travelled to the UK, only that they were approved to do so.

The most common type of visa people came to the UK on was study, which made up 53% of all visa entries from July 2025 to June 2026.

People from China were the most common group to come to the UK on study visas, making up 23% of the total.

Together, people from China and India accounted for nearly half of all study visas. This has been the case for many years.

The £10bn figure has been criticised by the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), which found a £115bn addition , external to UK public finances under current settlement rules.

"Public debate has focused heavily on the costs of recent migration, but this is not the whole story," IPPR associate director Marley Morris said.

Mahmood also declined to say whether Prime Minister Andy Burnham had told her to change tack on her proposals, which she had put forward in November under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

She told Today a public consultation had resulted in a "transformative package" that "strikes the right balance".

She has denied Monday's move was a U-turn, and said the revised plans meant some 500,000 people already in the UK would now have to wait longer than five years to qualify for settlement.

The exact wait will vary based on income and whether people arrived in the UK legally or illegally.

Mahmood had faced criticism within the Labour Party for proposing to retrospectively change the rules for migrant workers already in the UK.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner had said it amounted to "chang[ing] the goalposts" , while several MPs described the retrospective approach as "un-British" and warned it could worsen the UK's skills shortage, particularly in the care sector.
